knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polytope if and only if \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(S)\) for some finite set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of R^n is a polytope exactly when it is the convex hull of a finite set of vectors in R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is a polytope}\iff \exists S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ finite such that }Q=\operatorname{conv}(S).

children.title: Pure-Integer Hulls
children.top_down_role: Hull structure when every designated decision coordinate is integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Pure-Integer Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hull obtained when every decision coordinate is restricted to integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). Its pure-integer feasible set is \(S=P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\), and its pure-integer hull is
\[
P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
Thus \(P_I\) is the smallest convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) containing every integral point of \(P\). The definition does not by itself imply that \(P_I\) is closed or polyhedral; those properties require additional hypotheses such as rational polyhedrality of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pure-integer hull is the convex hull of all points of the original set whose coordinates are all integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\)

source_refs.locator: 1.4.2 Example: A Two-Dimensional Pure Integer Set p. 24

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4.2 Example: A Two-Dimensional Pure Integer Set p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer hull of one integral inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the exact convex hull of the integer points satisfying a single integral halfspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), \(g=\gcd(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\), and \(S=\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:ax\le c\}\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\frac{a}{g}x\le\left\lfloor\frac{c}{g}\right\rfloor\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer hull of a single inequality with a nonzero integral normal is obtained by dividing the normal by the gcd of its entries and rounding the correspondingly scaled right-hand side down.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\frac{a}{g}x\le\left\lfloor\frac{c}{g}\right\rfloor\right\}

children.title: Mixed-Integer Hulls
children.top_down_role: Hull structure relative to a selected integer-coordinate subspace.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{MI}=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(P\cap(\mathbb{Z}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q)\bigr)\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hull relative to a specified block of integer-constrained coordinates.

source_refs.locator: 1.4.1 Example: A Two-Dimensional Mixed Integer Set p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p,q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\), let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\), and write each point as \((z,y)\) with \(z\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\), where only \(z\) is required to be integral. The mixed-integer feasible set and mixed-integer hull are respectively
\[
S=P\cap(\mathbb{Z}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q),\qquad P_{MI}=\operatorname{conv}(S).
\]
When \(q=0\), this reduces to the pure-integer hull; when \(p=0\), it reduces to \(\operatorname{conv}(P)\), and hence to \(P\) whenever \(P\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed-integer hull is the convex hull of the points in the original set whose selected coordinate block is integral, while the remaining coordinates are continuous.

children.title: Rational Polyhedral Regime
children.top_down_role: The standard regime supporting finite rational descriptions of integer hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Polyhedral Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional rational-polyhedron version of integer-hull polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a rational polyhedron. For any coordinate index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the hull
\[
P_I=\operatorname{conv}\{x\in P:x_i\in\mathbb{Z}\text{ for every }i\in I\}
\]
is a rational polyhedron. Consequently, it admits a finite description by linear inequalities with rational coefficients. Taking \(I=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) gives the pure-integer case, while a proper subset gives the mixed-integer case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pure- or mixed-integer hull of a rational polyhedron is again a rational polyhedron and therefore has a finite rational inequality description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I\) is a rational polyhedron

children.title: Irrational-Data Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits caused by irrational polyhedral data.

knowledge_statements.title: Irrational-Data Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rationality cannot be omitted from the general integer-hull polyhedrality theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Rationality is a substantive hypothesis. For irrational \(\alpha>0\), consider the polyhedral cone
\[
C_\alpha=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x\ge0,\ y\ge\alpha x\}.
\]
Its defining data are irrational, and the lower boundary of \(\operatorname{conv}(C_\alpha\cap\mathbb{Z}^2)\) has infinitely many supporting segments associated with successive rational approximations to \(\alpha\). Hence the integer hull need not be a polyhedron after rationality of the original finite linear system is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An irrationally sloped cone can have an integer hull with infinitely many boundary segments, so rational-data polyhedrality does not extend to arbitrary real data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(C_\alpha\cap\mathbb{Z}^2)\) need not be polyhedral

notation.meaning: cone above the ray of irrational slope alpha

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and irrational-cone example fit the leaf, but the assertion about infinitely many supporting segments and its universal formulation for irrational alpha require an authoritative example or theorem locator.

children.title: Nonpolyhedral Integer Hulls
children.top_down_role: Integer hulls lacking a polyhedral representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonpolyhedral Integer Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-dimensional irrational cone exhibiting infinitely many integer-hull faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix irrational \(\alpha>0\) and let \(S_\alpha=\{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2:m\ge0,\ n\ge\alpha m\}\). The points on the lower convex envelope of \(S_\alpha\) include infinitely many best rational approximants to the ray \(y=\alpha x\). Their supporting-edge slopes converge to \(\alpha\) without becoming constant. Therefore
\[
H_\alpha=\operatorname{conv}(S_\alpha)
\]
has infinitely many distinct exposed edges and is not a polyhedron, although \(S_\alpha\) is obtained by imposing integrality on a cone described by two linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lattice points above an irrationally sloped ray have a convex hull with infinitely many exposed edges, providing a nonpolyhedral integer hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H_\alpha=\operatorname{conv}(S_\alpha)\) is not a polyhedron

notation.meaning: integer points on or above the irrational ray
convex hull of those integer points

children.title: Finite-Description Failure
children.top_down_role: Boundary cases where standard finite representation results cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Description Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite linear-inequality descriptions when an integer hull is nonpolyhedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For irrational \(\alpha>0\), let \(H_\alpha=\operatorname{conv}\{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2:m\ge0,\ n\ge\alpha m\}\). Since \(H_\alpha\) has infinitely many exposed edges, no finite family \((a^j,\beta_j)\), \(j=1,\ldots,k\), can satisfy
\[
H_\alpha=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:(a^j)^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta_j\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Thus finite inequality generation, and any representation requiring the integer hull itself to be a single finitely described polyhedron, fails in this irrational-data regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpolyhedral irrational integer hull cannot equal the solution set of finitely many linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no finite linear-inequality description of \(H_\alpha\)

notation.meaning: integer hull above the irrational ray

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:a finitely described linear-inequality set is polyhedral

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication from nonpolyhedrality to failure of a finite inequality description is standard and fits the failure-boundary leaf, but this record depends on an uncited irrational-hull counterexample.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite polytope-plus-integer-cone representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural representation of rational mixed-integer linear sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+p} be a rational polyhedron and S:=P\cap(\mathbb{Z}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p). There exist finitely many rational polytopes P_1,\ldots,P_k and vectors r^1,\ldots,r^q\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+p} such that S=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\left(P_i+\operatorname{intcone}\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\right).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every rational mixed-integer linear set is a finite union of rational polytopes plus one common finitely generated integer cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\left(P_i+\operatorname{intcone}\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\right)\text{ for finitely many rational polytopes }P_i\text{ and }r^j\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+p}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rational mixed-integer hull theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite rational description and recession behavior of a rational mixed-integer linear set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A,G and b be rational, P:=\{(x,y):Ax+Gy\le b\}, and S:=\{(x,y)\in P:x\text{ is integral}\}. Then there exist rational A',G',b' such that \operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,y):A'x+G'y\le b'\}. Moreover, if S\ne\varnothing, then \operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{conv}(S))=\operatorname{rec}(P).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the points of a rational polyhedron whose designated variables are integral is itself a rational polyhedron. If the mixed-integer set is nonempty, its convex hull and the original polyhedron have the same recession cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,y):A'x+G'y\le b'\}\text{ for some rational }A',G',b',\quad S\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{conv}(S))=\operatorname{rec}(P).

children.title: Integer-Hull Polyhedrality
children.top_down_role: Finite polyhedral structure of rational integer hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Polyhedrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-integer form of the fundamental rational integer-hull theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a rational polyhedron and suppose \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\ne\varnothing\). Then
\[
P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)
\]
is a rational polyhedron. In particular, finite rational sets \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{Q}^n\) exist such that
\[
P_I=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R),
\]
and equivalently finite rational matrices \(D\) and \(d\) exist with \(P_I=\{x:Dx\le d\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the integer points of a rational polyhedron is itself a finitely generated rational polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I\) is a rational polyhedron

notation.meaning: conic hull of the finite set R

children.title: Mixed-Integer Linear Representability
children.top_down_role: Projection and union structures representable by mixed-integer linear systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,y,z):Ax+By+Cz\le d,\ y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ z\in\mathbb{Z}^q\}\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based definition and unconditional basic closure properties of rational MILP-representable sets.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is rational mixed-integer linear representable if rational data \(A,B,C,d\) and dimensions \(p,q\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) exist such that
\[
S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ \exists z\in\mathbb{Z}^q,\ Ax+By+Cz\le d\}.
\]
Thus \(S\) is the projection onto the \(x\)-coordinates of a rational mixed-integer linear set. This class is closed under coordinate projections, finite intersections, and Cartesian products. No unconditional finite-union closure is asserted here; finite unions require additional representability conditions, such as the bounded-polyhedral construction treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational MILP-representable set is a projection of a rational linear system with continuous and integer auxiliary variables. Coordinate projections, finite intersections, and Cartesian products preserve this representation, while finite unions require additional conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Linear Representability

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of Mixed-Integer Linear Representable Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes mixed-integer linear representability using finitely many rational polytopes and a common finitely generated monoid of integer directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), the set \(S\) is mixed-integer linear representable if and only if there exist rational polytopes \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and vectors \(r^1,\ldots,r^t\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) such that
\[
S=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\left(P_i+\operatorname{intcone}\{r^1,\ldots,r^t\}\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is mixed-integer linear representable exactly when it is the union of finitely many rational polytopes, each added to the same monoid of nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many integer vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is mixed-integer linear representable}\iff\exists P_1,\ldots,P_k,\ r^1,\ldots,r^t\text{ as specified such that }S=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\left(P_i+\operatorname{intcone}\{r^1,\ldots,r^t\}\right).

children.title: Finite-Generation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Rationality and recession boundaries of finite representability.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Generation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite point-and-ray generation in the rational pure-integer regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a rational polyhedron with nonempty integer hull \(P_I\), then finite sets \(V\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) and \(R\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) may be chosen so that
\[
P_I=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R).
\]
The cone may be chosen equal to \(\operatorname{rec}(P_I)\), with integral generators obtained by scaling rational extreme rays. This finite-generation guarantee relies on rational polyhedrality; arbitrary irrational recession geometry or a nonpolyhedral hull lies outside its scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty rational integer hull is generated by finitely many integral points and integral recession rays; irrational nonpolyhedral cases need not admit such generation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for finite \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\)

notation.meaning: finite set of integral point generators
finite set of integral recession generators
recession cone of the integer hull

children.title: Finite-Union Representations
children.top_down_role: Integer-hull descriptions assembled from finitely many polyhedral pieces.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Union Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact selector formulation for a finite union of bounded rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let nonempty rational polytopes be given by \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_i x\le b_i\}\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\). Their union is the projection of the mixed-integer system
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^k x^i,\qquad A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i\ (i=1,\ldots,k),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\qquad \lambda_i\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Because exactly one selector equals one and each \(P_i\) is bounded, inactive blocks satisfy \(x^i=0\); consequently the projected set is exactly \(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union of rational polytopes has an exact lifted mixed-integer formulation using one binary selector per member.
assumptions_latex: \(P_i=\{x:A_i x\le b_i\}\) is a nonempty rational polytope for each \(i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(F)=\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\)

children.title: Projection Representations
children.top_down_role: Integer-hull descriptions obtained through elimination of auxiliary coordinates.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eliminating auxiliary coordinates preserves rational polyhedral and MILP representability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
Q=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{Z}^q:Ax+By+Cz\le d\},
\]
where all data are rational. Its coordinate projection is
\[
\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ \exists z\in\mathbb{Z}^q,\ Ax+By+Cz\le d\},
\]
which is mixed-integer linear representable. If \(q=0\), the projection is a rational polyhedron; it can be described by finitely many rational inequalities after eliminating \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting auxiliary variables from a rational MILP preserves MILP representability; without integer auxiliaries, projection preserves rational polyhedrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\) is rational MILP-representable, and is a rational polyhedron when \(q=0\)

children.title: Lifted-Union Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between disjunctive representations and lifted formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Union Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balas-type lifted interface connecting finite unions with their convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_i x\le b_i\}\), \(i=1,\ldots,k\), be nonempty polytopes. Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\right)=\left\{x:\begin{array}{l}x=\sum_{i=1}^k x^i,\ A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i\ (i=1,\ldots,k),\\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\ge0\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Here the displayed right-hand side denotes projection onto \(x\). Requiring \(\lambda_i\in\{0,1\}\) instead recovers the union itself; relaxing those selectors to the simplex produces its convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same lifted disjunctive system represents a union with binary selectors and its convex hull when those selectors are relaxed to a simplex.
assumptions_latex: \(P_i=\{x:A_i x\le b_i\}\) is a nonempty polytope for each \(i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(F_{\mathrm{simplex}})=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_I\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. An original-space description of \(P_I\) is a finite system
\[
Hx=h,\qquad Ax\le b,
\]
using only \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), such that
\[
P_I=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Hx=h,\ Ax\le b\}.
\]
The equations may be chosen to define \(\operatorname{aff}(P_I)\). Relative to that affine hull, an irredundant inequality subsystem contains exactly one inequality, up to positive scaling and addition of affine-hull equations, for each facet of \(P_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original-space description represents a nonempty integer-hull polyhedron exactly using affine-hull equations and finitely many inequalities in its original variables. Relative to the affine hull, an irredundant inequality subsystem has one inequality per facet.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Space Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear lifted formulations whose projection equals the original integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_I\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). An extended-space description of \(P_I\) is a polyhedron
\[
Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+q}:Ex+Fy\le g\}
\]
for some \(q\ge0\), satisfying
\[
P_I=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^q,\ Ex+Fy\le g\}.
\]
The variables \(y\) are auxiliary and need not have a unique value for a given \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended description introduces auxiliary variables and a polyhedron whose projection onto the original variables is exactly the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Description-Size Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of facet counts with the minimum size of a lifted formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a polytope \(P\), let \(f(P)\) be the number of facets in an irredundant original-space description, and define
\[
\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{m:\exists q\ge0,\ P=\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,y):Ex+Fy\le g\},\ g\in\mathbb R^m\}.
\]
Every original-space description is an extended description with \(q=0\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{xc}(P)\le f(P).
\]
Thus auxiliary variables may reduce the number of required inequalities, at the cost of increasing formulation dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension complexity never exceeds the original facet count; auxiliary variables can trade higher dimension for fewer inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\le f(P)\).

notation.meaning: number of facets of the polytope
minimum number of inequalities in an extended formulation

knowledge_statements.title: Faces of Integer Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed faces and their integer-point restriction representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(S=P\cap\mathbb Z^n\), and suppose \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is a polyhedron. A nonempty set \(F\subseteq P_I\) is a face of \(P_I\) if there exist \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \(a^Tx\le\beta\) is valid for \(P_I\) and
\[
F=\{x\in P_I:a^Tx=\beta\}.
\]
For this exposing inequality,
\[
F=\operatorname{conv}\{z\in S:a^Tz=\beta\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face of an integer hull is the equality set of a valid inequality and is the convex hull of the integer points attaining equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{conv}\{z\in S:a^Tz=\beta\}\).

notation.meaning: integer points of the underlying set
an exposed face of the integer hull

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edges, Extremal Rays, and Adjacency of Minimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General polyhedral facial geometry, including nonpointed polyhedra through their lineality space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron, let \(L=\operatorname{lin}(P)\) be its lineality space, and put \(t=\dim L\). A face \(G\) of dimension \(t+1\) has the form \(G=L+\ell\), where \(\ell\) is a line segment or a half-line, and has at most two facets, which are minimal faces of \(P\). If \(P\) is pointed, then \(G\) is called an edge when \(\ell\) is a line segment and an extremal ray when \(\ell\) is a half-line. Two minimal faces of \(P\) are adjacent (or neighboring) when they are contained in a common face of dimension \(t+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron whose lineality space has dimension t, each face of dimension t+1 is the sum of the lineality space and either a line segment or a half-line, and it has at most two facets, which are minimal faces. In a pointed polyhedron, these two cases are called an edge and an extremal ray, respectively. Two minimal faces are adjacent when a common face of dimension t+1 contains them.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a face of }P\text{ with }\dim G=t+1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G=L+\ell\text{ for a line segment or half-line }\ell,\quad G\text{ has at most two facets, each a minimal face of }P;\quad L=\{0\}\Rightarrow G\text{ is respectively an edge or an extremal ray.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization and dimensions of minimal faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal faces of a nonempty polyhedron represented by finitely many inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\neq\varnothing\). A nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\) is minimal if and only if there is a subsystem \(A'x\le b'\) of \(Ax\le b\) such that \(\operatorname{rank}(A')=\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A'x=b'\}\). Consequently, \(F\) is a translate of \(\operatorname{lin}(P)\). Moreover, the dimensions of the nonempty faces of \(P\) attain every integer value from \(\dim(\operatorname{lin}(P))\) through \(\dim(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty face is minimal exactly when it is the equality set of a subsystem having the same rank as the full defining matrix. Every minimal face is a translate of the lineality space, and nonempty face dimensions attain every integer between the lineality-space dimension and the polyhedron's dimension.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is a nonempty face of }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is minimal}\iff\exists(A'x\le b')\subseteq(Ax\le b):\operatorname{rank}(A')=\operatorname{rank}(A),\ F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A'x=b'\};\quad F\text{ is a translate of }\operatorname{lin}(P);\quad\{\dim G:G\text{ is a nonempty face of }P\}=\{d\in\mathbb{Z}:\dim(\operatorname{lin}(P))\le d\le\dim(P)\}

knowledge_statements.title: Facets of Integer Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codimension-one proper faces of an integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_I\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be an integer-hull polyhedron of affine dimension \(d\ge1\). A face \(F\) of \(P_I\) is a facet if
\[
\dim(F)=d-1.
\]
Equivalently, a valid inequality \(a^Tx\le\beta\) defines a facet when the equality set \(F=\{x\in P_I:a^Tx=\beta\}\) contains \(d\) affinely independent points. Facet-defining inequalities are considered identical when one is a positive scalar multiple of the other on \(\operatorname{aff}(P_I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facet is a proper integer-hull face of codimension one, equivalently an equality face containing enough affinely independent points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a facet exactly when \(\dim(F)=d-1\).

notation.meaning: affine dimension of the integer hull
face defined by equality in a valid inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General facet characterization for a full-dimensional polytope given by finite generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite set of vectors and let \(P=\operatorname{conv}(S)\) be full-dimensional. cx\le\delta\text{ is an inequality in the ambient space}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: cx\le\delta\text{ determines a facet of }P\iff \left[\forall x\in S,\ cx\le\delta\right]\land\left[\forall a\notin\{\lambda c:\lambda\ge0\},\ \exists x',x''\in S:\ ax'<ax'',\ cx'=\delta\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face Induced by an Irredundant Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial structure induced by an irredundant, non-implicit inequality in a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), with implicit-equality indices \(I^=\) and remaining indices \(I^<\). Suppose \(j\in I^<\), the inequality \(a^jx\le b_j\) is irredundant, and \(F=\{x\in P:a^jx=b_j\}\). Then (i) there is \(\widehat x\in F\) such that \(a^i\widehat x<b_i\) for every \(i\in I^<\setminus\{j\}\); (ii) \(\operatorname{aff}(F)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^ix=b_i\ (i\in I^=\cup\{j\})\}\); and (iii) \(\dim F=\dim P-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The face defined by an irredundant non-implicit inequality contains a point where every other non-implicit inequality is strict. Its affine hull is obtained by adding that inequality to the implicit equalities, and its dimension is one less than that of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\widehat x\in F\;\forall i\in I^<\setminus\{j\}:a^i\widehat x<b_i,\quad \operatorname{aff}(F)=\{x:a^ix=b_i\ (i\in I^=\cup\{j\})\},\quad \dim F=\dim P-1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of Polyhedral Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facet characterization for a nonempty polyhedron and correspondence with inequalities in a minimal representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing\), and let \(f\) be its number of facets. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness of Minimal Polyhedral Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of two minimal representations of a nonempty, possibly lower-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(k=\dim P\), and let \(f\) be its number of facets. Suppose \(A^=x=b^=,\ A^<x\le b^<\) and \(C^=x=d^=,\ C^<x\le d^<\) are minimal representations of \(P\). Each equality system has \(n-k\) equations, and every equation of the second has the form \((uA^=)x=ub^=\) for some \(u\in\mathbb R^{n-k}\). Each inequality system has \(f\) inequalities. After permuting their indices, for every \(j=1,\ldots,f\) there are \(\lambda_j>0\) and \(u_j\in\mathbb R^{n-k}\) such that \(c^j=\lambda_j a^j+u_jA^=\) and \(d_j=\lambda_jb_j+u_jb^=\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two minimal representations of a nonempty polyhedron have codimension-many equality rows and facet-many inequality rows. Their equality systems describe the same affine hull, while corresponding facet inequalities differ by positive scaling and the addition of equations valid throughout the polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: A^=x=b^=,\ A^<x\le b^<\text{ and }C^=x=d^=,\ C^<x\le d^<\text{ are minimal representations of }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: m_{A^=}=m_{C^=}=n-k,\quad m_{A^<}=m_{C^<}=f,\quad c^j=\lambda_j a^j+u_jA^=,\quad d_j=\lambda_jb_j+u_jb^=\text{ after permutation, with }\lambda_j>0.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Adjacency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacency through one-dimensional faces of the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_I\) be a polyhedron and let \(u\ne v\) be vertices of \(P_I\). The vertices \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent if their segment
\[
[u,v]=\{(1-\lambda)u+\lambda v:0\le\lambda\le1\}
\]
is a one-dimensional face of \(P_I\). Equivalently, the smallest face of \(P_I\) containing both \(u\) and \(v\) has dimension one; that face is then exactly \([u,v]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two integer-hull vertices are adjacent exactly when their joining segment is an edge, or equivalently their smallest common face is one-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent if and only if \([u,v]\) is a one-dimensional face of \(P_I\).

children.title: Facet Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial adjacency among facets of integer hulls.

knowledge_statements.title: Facet Adjacency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjacency through codimension-two intersections in the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_I\) be a polyhedron of affine dimension \(d\ge2\), and let \(F_1\ne F_2\) be facets of \(P_I\). The facets are adjacent if their intersection is a ridge, namely a face of dimension \(d-2\):
\[
F_1\sim F_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \dim(F_1\cap F_2)=d-2.
\]
If the intersection is empty or has dimension less than \(d-2\), the facets are not adjacent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two distinct facets are adjacent precisely when their intersection is a codimension-two face of the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1\sim F_2\) if and only if \(\dim(F_1\cap F_2)=d-2\).

notation.meaning: affine dimension of the integer hull

children.title: Vertex-Facet Incidence Consequences

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Facet Incidence Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of common faces and adjacency from vertex-facet incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_I\) be a polytope and let \(u,v\) be distinct vertices. The smallest face containing \(u\) and \(v\) is
\[
G(u,v)=\bigcap\{F:F\text{ is a facet of }P_I,\ u\in F,\ v\in F\},
\]
where an empty intersection is interpreted as \(P_I\). Consequently, \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent exactly when \(\dim G(u,v)=1\). More generally, the facets containing a nonempty proper face intersect exactly in that face, so vertex-facet incidence determines the face lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common incident facets determine the smallest face containing given vertices; their intersection therefore yields a vertex-adjacency test and the polytope's face lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) are adjacent if and only if \(\dim G(u,v)=1\).

notation.meaning: intersection of all facets incident to both vertices

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of all extreme points of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is vertex-integral if every vertex of \(P\) belongs to the integer lattice:
\[
\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb Z^n.
\]
Equivalently, for every vertex \(v\) of \(P\), all coordinates of \(v\) are integers. This predicate concerns vertices only; without additional hypotheses, it does not by itself specify the recession or lineality structure of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is vertex-integral when every one of its vertices has integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is vertex-integral if and only if \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\).

notation.meaning: set of vertices of the polyhedron

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of a vertex
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex characterizations for a pointed polyhedron represented by linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a pointed polyhedron and let \(\bar{x}\in P\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(\bar{x}\) is a vertex of \(P\); (ii) \(\bar{x}\) satisfies at equality \(n\) linearly independent inequalities of \(Ax\le b\); (iii) there are no distinct \(x',x''\in P\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\) such that \(\bar{x}=\lambda x'+(1-\lambda)x''\).

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Face Integrality Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence for rational pointed polyhedra, excluding vacuous vertex conditions caused by lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty rational pointed polyhedron. Then the following are equivalent:
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n);
\]
\[
\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb Z^n;
\]
\[
F=\operatorname{conv}(F\cap\mathbb Z^n)\quad\text{for every nonempty face }F\text{ of }P.
\]
Thus, under rationality and pointedness, integrality of the entire polyhedron, integrality of all vertices, and integrality of all nonempty faces coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty rational pointed polyhedron, whole-polyhedron integrality, integer vertices, and integrality of every nonempty face are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, rational, and pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is integral}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\Longleftrightarrow\text{every nonempty face of }P\text{ is integral}.\)

notation.meaning: set of vertices of the polyhedron
a nonempty face of the polyhedron

knowledge_statements.title: Box Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard definition using integer-coordinate boxes, allowing infinite endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron. An integer box is \(B(l,u)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:l_i\le x_i\le u_i\text{ for all }i\}\), where \(l,u\in(\mathbb{Z}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\})^n\) and \(l_i\le u_i\). The polyhedron \(P\) is box-integral if, for every integer box \(B(l,u)\), the intersection satisfies \[P\cap B(l,u)=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\cap B(l,u))\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\bigr),\] with the empty intersection regarded as integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron is box-integral when every intersection with an integer-coordinate box equals the convex hull of its integer points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\cap B(l,u)=\operatorname{conv}((P\cap B(l,u))\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\) for every integer box \(B(l,u)\).

notation.meaning: Integer-coordinate box with possibly infinite endpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality relative to the lattice induced on a rational affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a rational affine subspace with \(A\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\ne\varnothing\), and let \(P\subseteq A\) be a polyhedron. Write \(\Lambda_A=A\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\). The polyhedron \(P\) is integral relative to \(A\) if \[P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\Lambda_A).\] Equivalently, after choosing any integer point \(a_0\in A\), integrality is measured in the translated lattice \((A-a_0)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\) inside the linear space \(A-a_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative integrality means that a polyhedron in an affine subspace is generated convexly by the ambient integer lattice points lying in that subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\Lambda_A)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Subspace Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-subspace condition pairing integer fixings with bounded integer boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has bounded-subspace compatibility if, for every \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), every \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^{\bar I}\), and all \(l,u\in\mathbb{Z}^{I}\) with \(l\le u\), the section \[S=\{x\in P:x_{\bar I}=z,\ l_i\le x_i\le u_i\text{ for }i\in I\}\] is empty or integral, namely \(S=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\). This predicate tests compatibility of integrality with integer coordinate fixings and bounded free-coordinate boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bounded coordinate section obtained by integer fixings and integer bounds must be empty or the convex hull of its integer points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\varnothing\) or \(S=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Sections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate sections preserved by box integrality under integer fixings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be box-integral. Choose \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a vector \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^{I}\), and bounds \(l_j,u_j\in\mathbb{Z}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\) satisfying \(l_j\le u_j\) for every \(j\notin I\). Then the coordinate section \[S=P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_i=z_i\text{ for }i\in I,\ l_j\le x_j\le u_j\text{ for }j\notin I\}\] is integral whenever it is nonempty. Thus integer coordinate equations preserve integrality after any simultaneous integer-box restriction covered by box integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-integral polyhedron remains integral after fixing coordinates to integers and imposing integer or infinite bounds on the remaining coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^{I}\), and \(l_j,u_j\in\mathbb{Z}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\) with \(l_j\le u_j\) for every \(j\notin I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\) whenever \(S\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality is preserved and reflected by nonempty Cartesian products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) be nonempty polyhedra. Their Cartesian product is integral with respect to \(\mathbb{Z}^{p+q}\) if and only if both factors are integral with respect to their coordinate lattices: \[P\times Q=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\times Q)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{p+q}\bigr)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^p)\text{ and }Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^q).\] The nonemptiness assumption excludes vacuous recovery of a factor from an empty product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty Cartesian product of polyhedra is integral exactly when each factor is integral in its own integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\times Q\) is integral if and only if \(P\) and \(Q\) are integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Preservation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-affine images preserve integrality; non-lattice-preserving maps need not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be integral and let \(T(x)=Mx+t\), where \(M\in\mathbb{Z}^{k\times n}\) and \(t\in\mathbb{Z}^k\). Then \[T(P)=\operatorname{conv}(T(P)\cap\mathbb{Z}^k),\] so coordinate projections preserve integrality. The integer-affine hypothesis is essential: for the integral polyhedron \(P=\{1\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and the rational map \(T(x)=x/2\), the image \(T(P)=\{1/2\}\) contains no integer point and is not integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer-affine projections preserve integrality, but a rational map can send an integral singleton to a nonintegral singleton.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(P)\) is integral; preservation can fail when \(T(\mathbb{Z}^n)\nsubseteq\mathbb{Z}^k\).

notation.meaning: Affine map between the ambient spaces.

children.title: Aggregation Preservation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Preservation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative row aggregation can destroy integrality when it replaces the original system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integral polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:x\le1,\ -x\le0\}=[0,1]\) is defined by two integral inequalities. Replacing both inequalities by their nonnegative aggregate, obtained with multipliers \(1\) and \(1/4\), gives \[(3/4)x\le1,\] whose feasible region is \(R=(-\infty,4/3]\). Since \(R\cap\mathbb{Z}=\{z\in\mathbb{Z}:z\le1\}\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(R\cap\mathbb{Z})=(-\infty,1]\ne R\), the aggregated relaxation is not integral. Thus aggregation is not integrality-preserving when the original rows are discarded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing an integral system by a valid nonnegative aggregation may produce a relaxation with a fractional extreme point and destroy integrality.
assumptions_latex: The inequalities \(x\le1\) and \(-x\le0\) are replaced by the aggregate formed with nonnegative multipliers \(1\) and \(1/4\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is integral, whereas \(R=(-\infty,4/3]\) is not integral.

notation.meaning: Feasible region of the aggregated inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Counterexamples
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent projected formulations can have different integrality under different lattice assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integral interval \(P=[0,1]\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) has the extended reformulation \[Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x=2y,\ 0\le y\le1/2\}.\] Its projection onto the \(x\)-coordinate is exactly \(P\), but \(Q\) is not integral with respect to \(\mathbb{Z}^2\): its endpoints are \((0,0)\) and \((1,1/2)\), while \(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^2=\{(0,0)\}\). Hence continuous equivalence after projection does not preserve full-space integrality when auxiliary-variable lattice status changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended formulation can project to an integral set yet be nonintegral in its full variable space because an auxiliary endpoint is fractional.
assumptions_latex: Integrality of the extended space is measured with respect to \(\mathbb{Z}^2\).
Only equality of the projected continuous feasible sets is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=P\), but \(Q\ne\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb{Z}^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Solution Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial certificate length for rational integer-linear feasibility and finite optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider integer data \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), and optionally \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), with total binary encoding length \(L\). There is a polynomial \(p\) such that, whenever \(\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is nonempty, it contains a point whose binary encoding length is at most \(p(L)\). If \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}\) has a finite optimum, an optimal integer point can likewise be chosen with encoding length at most \(p(L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible integer linear system, and any finite integer optimum, admits a solution whose binary description is polynomial in the input length.
assumptions_latex: \(A,b\), and when present \(c\), are integer data encoded in binary.
The integer feasible set is nonempty; the optimization variant has finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{size}(x)\le p(L)\) for some feasible, or respectively optimal, integer point \(x\).

notation.meaning: Total binary encoding length of the input data.
A polynomial independent of the particular encoded instance.

children.title: Proximity Principles
children.top_down_role: Distance relationships between continuous and integer solution geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximity Principles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical linear-programming versus integer-programming proximity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Suppose the linear program \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b\}\) has an optimal vertex \(x^*\), and the corresponding integer program is feasible with finite optimum. If \(\Delta(A)\) is the largest absolute determinant of any square submatrix of \(A\), then there exists an optimal integer solution \(z^*\) satisfying \[\lVert x^*-z^*\rVert_\infty\le n\Delta(A).\] Thus an optimal integer point lies in a determinant-controlled neighborhood of every chosen optimal LP vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal integer solution can be chosen within infinity-distance n times the maximum subdeterminant from an optimal LP vertex.

knowledge_statements.title: Doignon–Helly Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Doignon's integer Helly theorem for finite families of convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}=\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\) be a finite family of convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). If every subfamily of at most \(2^n\) members has an intersection containing a point of \(\mathbb{Z}^n\), then \[\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\ne\varnothing.\] Equivalently, if the full intersection contains no integer point, some subfamily of at most \(2^n\) sets already has integer-point-free intersection. The constant \(2^n\) is the Helly number of \(\mathbb{Z}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer infeasibility of a finite convex family in n dimensions is witnessed by at most 2^n of its members.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite integer-generator version with a norm-dependent support bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) be finite, let \(M:=\max_{x\in X}\|x\|_\infty\ge1\), and suppose \(b\in\operatorname{intcone}(X)\). Then there is a subset \(Y\subseteq X\) and coefficients \(\mu_y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) such that
\[
b=\sum_{y\in Y}\mu_y y
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
|Y|\le 2d\log_2(4dM).
\]
Thus every integer-conic representation admits another representation using only a dimension- and magnitude-controlled number of distinct generators; the coefficients themselves need not be bounded by this assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer-cone element generated by bounded integer vectors can be represented using at most a dimension- and magnitude-dependent number of distinct generators.

children.title: Flatness Phenomena
children.top_down_role: Geometric thinness regimes relevant to lattice-point structure.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a full-dimensional closed convex body.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(K)\le F(d)\) for a finite constant depending only on \(d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean flatness theorem for convex bodies avoiding the integer lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every integer \(d\ge1\), there exists a finite constant \(F(d)\) such that every full-dimensional closed convex body \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(K\cap\mathbb Z^d=\varnothing\) obeys
\[
w(K):=\min_{0\ne a\in\mathbb Z^d}\left(\sup_{x\in K}a^\top x-\inf_{x\in K}a^\top x\right)\le F(d).
\]
Equivalently, every lattice-free convex body is thin, in at least one nonzero integral direction, by an amount bounded solely as a function of the ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every full-dimensional convex body containing no integer point has bounded width in some nonzero integral direction, with the bound depending only on dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Flatness Phenomena

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement has the correct theorem role and local sense, but the existence and precise scope of the flatness constant are unsupported because no source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Lattice-Width Parameters
children.top_down_role: Directional width measures relative to the integer lattice.

assumptions_latex: The directional extrema are interpreted in \(\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w(K)=\inf_{0\ne a\in\mathbb Z^d}w_a(K)\), with the minimum attained when \(K\) is compact.

notation.meaning: Width of K in integral direction a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard width relative to the lattice \(\mathbb Z^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and a nonzero integral vector \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\), define its directional width by
\[
w_a(K):=\sup_{x\in K}a^\top x-\inf_{x\in K}a^\top x.
\]
The lattice width of \(K\) relative to \(\mathbb Z^d\) is
\[
w(K):=\inf_{0\ne a\in\mathbb Z^d}w_a(K).
\]
If \(K\) is compact, each directional width is finite and the infimum over primitive integral directions is attained, so it may be written as a minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lattice width is the least distance, measured by an integral linear functional, between two parallel supporting hyperplanes of a set.
knowledge_statements.title: Lattice-Width Parameters

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of directional and lattice width is standard, but the assertion that the infimum is attained for every compact set is false without additional conditions such as full dimensionality. A lower-dimensional compact set in an irrational direction can have infimum zero without an attaining integral direction. No source is supplied to settle the intended scope.

children.title: Dimension-Sensitive Width Bounds
children.top_down_role: Dependence of width structure on ambient dimension.

assumptions_latex: \(F(d)\) is the supremal lattice width of full-dimensional convex bodies in \(\mathbb R^d\) avoiding \(\mathbb Z^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that \(F(d)\le Cd^{3/2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical asymptotic upper bound for the Euclidean flatness constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
F(d):=\sup\{w(K):K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ is a full-dimensional convex body and }K\cap\mathbb Z^d=\varnothing\}.
\]
There exists an absolute constant \(C>0\), independent of \(d\), such that
\[
F(d)\le C d^{3/2}
\]
for every integer \(d\ge1\). Consequently, a lattice-free convex body in dimension \(d\) has width at most order \(d^{3/2}\) in some nonzero integral direction. This is an asymptotic bound and does not specify the optimal constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flatness constant grows no faster than a constant times dimension to the three-halves power, yielding a dimension-sensitive thin direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Sensitive Width Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asymptotic upper bound is a theorem about a geometric parameter, not a computational complexity bound. Moreover, no source identifies the precise classical bound or its hypotheses, so the stated exponent cannot be accepted from the supplied evidence.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\in\mathbb Z^{d\times d}\) be nonsingular. There is a unimodular matrix \(U\in\mathbb Z^{d\times d}\) such that \(H:=BU\) is upper triangular and satisfies
\[
h_{ii}>0,
\qquad
0\le h_{ij}<h_{ii}\quad(1\le i<j\le d).
\]
Under this column convention, \(H\) is uniquely determined by the lattice \(B\mathbb Z^d\), although \(U\) need not be unique. Hence two nonsingular integer basis matrices generate the same lattice exactly when their column Hermite normal forms coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every full-rank integer lattice has a unique upper-triangular, residue-reduced basis obtained by a unimodular integer change of columns.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive Groups, Generated Groups, and Lattices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational lattice terminology in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is an additive group if \(0\in\Lambda\) and, for all \(x,y\in\Lambda\), both \(x+y\in\Lambda\) and \(-x\in\Lambda\). It is generated by \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) if \(\Lambda=\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i a_i:\lambda_i\in\mathbb Z\}\). Such a group is a lattice if it can be generated by linearly independent vectors; those vectors form a basis of the lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An additive group in Euclidean space contains zero and is closed under addition and negation. It is generated by given vectors when it consists of all their integer linear combinations. It is a lattice when it has a linearly independent generating set, called a lattice basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda\) is a lattice precisely when \(\Lambda=\{\sum_i\lambda_i b_i:\lambda_i\in\mathbb Z\}\) for some linearly independent vectors \(b_i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hermite-Normal-Form Criterion for Integer Linear Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer solvability and complete solution parametrization for a full-row-rank rational coefficient matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(H=(D\;0)=AU\) be the Hermite normal form of \(A\), where \(U\) is unimodular. When this holds, all integer solutions are \(\left\{U\binom{\bar y}{k}:k\in\mathbb Z^{n-m}\right\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solving Linear Diophantine Systems by Hermite Normal Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank reduction, Hermite-normal-form transformation, integer-feasibility testing, and recovery of a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To solve \(Ax=b\) over \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\), first test whether \(A\) has full row rank. If not, detect inconsistency or remove redundant equations. Transform the resulting full-row-rank matrix by unimodular operations to \(H=AU\), where \(H\) is in Hermite normal form and \(U\) is unimodular. Solve \(Hy=b\) over \(y\in\mathbb Z^n\). If it is infeasible, then \(Ax=b\) has no integer solution; otherwise, for an integer solution \(\bar y\), return \(\bar x=U\bar y\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmented-Matrix Column Algorithm for Hermite Normal Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional algorithmic statement using the preceding construction of the augmented matrix A' and the parameter M, which are not defined independently in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A' and M be as in the preceding construction, with \operatorname{HNF}(A')=[\operatorname{HNF}(A)\;0] and with auxiliary columns that permit the stated entry reductions. At a stage where B is lower triangular and the first row of D=(\delta_{ij}) is nonzero, whenever \delta_{1i}\geq\delta_{1j}>0 for i\neq j, subtract \left\lfloor\delta_{1i}/\delta_{1j}\right\rfloor times column j from column i and then use the auxiliary columns to reduce the relevant entries between 0 and M. Repeat until the first row of D has exactly one nonzero entry, enlarge B, and continue. When B is the final lower-triangular block, add integral multiples of column i to each earlier column j<i so that 0\leq\beta_{ij}<\beta_{ii}. Deleting the final m auxiliary columns yields \operatorname{HNF}(A).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the preceding augmented-matrix construction, apply Euclidean column reductions to the first row of the residual block, restore the prescribed entry bounds using auxiliary columns, and enlarge the triangular block whenever one nonzero remains. Normalize the resulting lower-triangular block and delete the auxiliary columns to obtain the Hermite normal form of A.
assumptions_latex: A'\text{ and }M\text{ are constructed as in the preceding method}
B\text{ is the current lower-triangular block}
D=(\delta_{ij})\text{ has a nonzero first row}
\text{The auxiliary columns permit the stated reductions of entries between }0\text{ and }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Deleting the final }m\text{ auxiliary columns yields }\operatorname{HNF}(A).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) of rank \(r\), there exist unimodular matrices \(U\in\mathbb Z^{m\times m}\) and \(V\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) such that
\[
UAV=D:=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0),
\qquad
0<d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_r.
\]
The positive integers \(d_1,\ldots,d_r\) are uniquely determined by \(A\). Moreover, the cokernel has the decomposition
\[
\mathbb Z^m/A\mathbb Z^n\cong
\bigoplus_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z/d_i\mathbb Z\ \oplus\ \mathbb Z^{m-r}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unimodular row and column operations diagonalize any integer matrix into uniquely determined divisibility-ordered invariant factors describing its cokernel.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and uniqueness of Smith normal form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational matrices under elementary integral row and column operations, equivalently unimodular transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) have rank \(k\). Elementary row and column operations transform \(A\) into \[\begin{bmatrix}D&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_k),\] where \(\delta_i>0\) and \(\delta_1\mid\delta_2\mid\cdots\mid\delta_k\). This form is unique, and for every \(1\le i\le k\), \(\delta_1\cdots\delta_i\) equals the greatest common divisor of the order-\(i\) minors of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every rational matrix has a unique Smith normal form with positive diagonal entries forming a divisibility chain. The product of the first i diagonal entries equals the greatest common divisor of its i-by-i minors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\sim\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_k)&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad \delta_1\mid\cdots\mid\delta_k,\quad \prod_{j=1}^i\delta_j=\gcd\{\det M:M\text{ is an }i\times i\text{ minor of }A\}.

source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\in\mathbb Z^{d\times d}\) be nonsingular with \(|b_{ij}|\le M\) and \(M\ge1\), and let \(H\) be its column Hermite normal form. Hadamard's determinant bound gives
\[
|\det B|\le d^{d/2}M^d.
\]
Because the diagonal entries of \(H\) are positive with product \(|\det B|\), and every reduced off-diagonal entry is smaller than its row pivot, each entry of \(H\) requires \(O(d(\log d+\log M))\) binary bits. Thus the complete encoding length of \(H\) is polynomial in the binary encoding length of \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hermite normal form of a bounded full-rank integer matrix has polynomial binary encoding length; determinant bounds control every reduced entry.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Form Encoding Size

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(UAV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0)\) be a Smith normal form and set \(c:=Ub\). The system \(Ax=b\) has an integer solution if and only if
\[
d_i\mid c_i\quad(1\le i\le r),
\qquad
c_i=0\quad(r<i\le m).
\]
When these tests hold, set \(y_i=c_i/d_i\) for \(i\le r\) and choose the remaining coordinates integrally, for example as zero; then \(x:=Vy\) satisfies \(Ax=b\). The displayed normal-form identity, divisibility tests, and multiplication \(Ax=b\) are directly checkable certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smith normal form reduces integer-system solvability to divisibility and zero tests; a transformed quotient vector yields a verifiable integer solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Solvability Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L:=B\mathbb Z^d\), where \(B\in\mathbb Z^{d\times d}\) is nonsingular, and let \(H\) be its column Hermite normal form. For any \(b\in\mathbb Z^d\), triangular back substitution produces the unique rational vector \(z\in\mathbb Q^d\) satisfying \(Hz=b\). Then
\[
b\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z\in\mathbb Z^d.
\]
For a yes-instance, the integral vector \(z\) is a membership certificate verified by checking \(Hz=b\). The equality \(H\mathbb Z^d=B\mathbb Z^d\) ensures that this check certifies membership in the original lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector belongs to a full-rank integer lattice exactly when its coordinates in the Hermite basis are integral; those coordinates certify membership.
knowledge_statements.title: Membership Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r\), choose unimodular \(U,V\) with
\[
UAV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0),
\]
and set \(c:=Ub\). Since \(V^{-1}\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb Z^n\), the equation \(Ax=b\) is solvable in \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) if and only if \(Dy=c\) is solvable in \(y\in\mathbb Z^n\). Equivalently,
\[
d_i\mid c_i\quad(1\le i\le r),
\qquad c_i=0\quad(r<i\le m).
\]
These conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-row-rank rational linear systems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-lattice membership criterion for an arbitrary rectangular integer matrix.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Theory of lattices and linear diophantine equations p. 45
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), define its column lattice by
\[
L(A):=A\mathbb Z^n=\{Az:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}.
\]
Let \(UAV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0)\) be a Smith normal form and let \(c:=Ub\). Then
\[
b\in L(A)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d_i\mid c_i\ \text{ for }1\le i\le r
\ \text{ and }\ c_i=0\ \text{ for }r<i\le m.
\]
Thus lattice membership is precisely the solvability of the associated integer equation \(Az=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Membership in an integer column lattice is equivalent to divisibility by every nonzero Smith invariant and vanishing in the remaining transformed coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Lattice Membership

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(UAV=D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_r,0)\) and \(c:=Ub\). Integer infeasibility of \(Ax=b\) is certified by either an index \(i>r\) with \(c_i\ne0\), or an index \(i\le r\) with \(d_i\nmid c_i\). A verifier checks that \(U\) and \(V\) are unimodular, that \(UAV=D\), that \(c=Ub\), and that the indicated obstruction holds. Since every integer solution would transform into an integer solution of \(Dy=c\), either obstruction certifies that no \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) can satisfy \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero coordinate beyond the rank or a failed Smith-factor divisibility test provides a directly verifiable certificate of integer infeasibility.

children.title: Congruence Systems
children.top_down_role: Modular representations of integer feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Congruence Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-modulus linear congruences over integer vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and \(q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\). The congruence system \(Ax\equiv b\pmod q\) consists of all \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfying \(a_i^\top x-b_i\in q\mathbb Z\) for every row \(i\). Equivalently,
\[
Ax\equiv b\pmod q\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in\mathbb Z^m:\ Ax-qy=b.
\]
Thus a linear congruence system is representable as a linear Diophantine system with auxiliary integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A modular linear system is equivalent to an ordinary integer linear system after introducing one integer quotient variable per congruence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\equiv b\pmod q\iff b\in A\mathbb Z^n+q\mathbb Z^m\).

children.title: Affine Lattice Cosets
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization of inhomogeneous Diophantine solution sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Lattice Cosets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coset representation of a nonempty integer solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and suppose \(x^0\in\mathbb Z^n\) satisfies \(Ax^0=b\). With \(L=\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n\), the complete integer solution set is
\[
\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b\}=x^0+L=\{x^0+z:z\in L\}.
\]
The set is independent of the selected particular solution: if \(x^1\) is another integer solution, then \(x^1-x^0\in L\), so \(x^1+L=x^0+L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty inhomogeneous integer linear solution set is one affine coset of the homogeneous integer kernel lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax=b\}=x^0+(\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n)\).

notation.meaning: affine lattice coset through a particular solution

children.title: Integer Kernel Lattices
children.top_down_role: Lattice structure of homogeneous integer equations.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Kernel Lattices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous integer kernel and its lattice rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), its integer kernel lattice is
\[
L_A=\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n=\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:Az=0\}.
\]
If \(r=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Q}(A)\), then \(L_A\) is a free abelian group of rank \(n-r\), and its real span equals \(\ker(A)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Consequently, there exists an integer matrix \(B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times(n-r)}\) with linearly independent columns such that \(L_A=B\mathbb Z^{n-r}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer solutions of a homogeneous integral system form a lattice whose rank equals the real kernel dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_A\cong\mathbb Z^{n-r}\) and \(\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(L_A)=\ker(A)\).

notation.meaning: integer basis matrix for the lattice

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Circuits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primitive support-minimal integer dependencies among matrix columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), a circuit vector is a nonzero \(g\in\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n\) such that no nonzero \(h\in\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n\) has \(\operatorname{supp}(h)\subsetneq\operatorname{supp}(g)\), and \(\gcd\{|g_i|:g_i\ne0\}=1\). A matrix circuit is the signed pair \(\{g,-g\}\), or a single representative after fixing a sign convention. Its support is a minimally linearly dependent set of columns of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix circuit is a primitive integer kernel vector with inclusion-minimal support, considered up to sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is a circuit vector exactly when it is primitive and support-minimal in \((\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n)\setminus\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: indices of nonzero coordinates of g

children.title: Elementary Kernel Vectors
children.top_down_role: Primitive support-minimal vectors in integer kernels.

knowledge_statements.title: Elementary Kernel Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary directions in the real kernel of an integer matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\). A nonzero vector \(v\in\ker(A)\) is elementary if there is no nonzero \(w\in\ker(A)\) satisfying \(\operatorname{supp}(w)\subsetneq\operatorname{supp}(v)\). Elementary vectors are considered up to nonzero scalar multiplication. Because \(A\) is integral, every elementary one-dimensional direction contains a unique pair \(\{g,-g\}\) of primitive integer vectors. These primitive representatives are precisely the circuit vectors of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elementary kernel vectors are nonzero kernel directions having minimal support; their primitive integer representatives are matrix circuits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is elementary if and only if its direction has a primitive integer representative that is a circuit vector of \(A\).

notation.meaning: indices of nonzero coordinates of v

children.title: Support-Minimal Direction Relations
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences between circuit representations and elementary directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Support-Minimal Direction Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between minimal column dependencies and minimal kernel supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[a_1\ \cdots\ a_n]\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and let \(0\ne v\in\ker(A)\). Set \(S=\operatorname{supp}(v)\). Then \(v\) is support-minimal in \(\ker(A)\setminus\{0\}\) if and only if \(\{a_i:i\in S\}\) is linearly dependent and every proper subset is linearly independent. In that case, the subspace \(\{w\in\ker(A):\operatorname{supp}(w)\subseteq S\}\) is one-dimensional, so all kernel relations supported on \(S\) are scalar multiples of \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal supports of nonzero kernel vectors coincide with minimally dependent column sets, and each such support determines one kernel direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is support-minimal if and only if \(\operatorname{supp}(v)\) indexes a minimally dependent column set of \(A\).

notation.meaning: support of the kernel vector v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Improving-direction certificates for a fixed constraint matrix and objective class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) and a class \(\mathcal C\) of objective functions on \(\mathbb Z^n\). A finite set \(T\subseteq(\ker(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n)\setminus\{0\}\) is a test set for \((A,\mathcal C)\) if, for every \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), every \(c\in\mathcal C\), and every feasible but nonoptimal \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^n\) with \(Ax=b\), some \(t\in T\) satisfies \(x+t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^n\), \(A(x+t)=b\), and \(c(x+t)<c(x)\). Absence of such an improving move therefore certifies global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite test set supplies a feasible improving kernel move from every nonoptimal integer point; no improving move certifies optimality.

children.title: Unimodular Coordinate Changes
children.top_down_role: Integrality-preserving transformations of lattices and integer systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Unimodular Coordinate Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral changes of coordinates preserving lattice membership and determinants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A square integer matrix \(U\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) is unimodular when \(\det(U)=\pm1\), equivalently when \(U^{-1}\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\). The map \(z\mapsto Uz\) is then a bijection of \(\mathbb Z^n\). For any lattice basis matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), matrices \(B\) and \(BU\) generate the same lattice:
\[
BU\mathbb Z^n=B\mathbb Z^n.
\]
Likewise, substituting \(x=Uy\) transforms \(Ax=b\) into \(AUy=b\) without changing integer feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unimodular matrix bijectively changes integer coordinates, preserves lattice points, and replaces a basis without changing its lattice.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has linearly independent columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb Z^n\) and \(BU\mathbb Z^n=B\mathbb Z^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) and \(A'\) be nonsingular square matrices of the same order. The following are equivalent: (i) their columns generate the same lattice; (ii) \(A'\) is obtainable from \(A\) by elementary column operations; and (iii) \(A'=AU\) for some unimodular matrix \(U\), equivalently \(A^{-1}A'\) is unimodular.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(A)=L(A')\iff A'\text{ is obtainable from }A\text{ by elementary column operations}\iff \exists U\text{ unimodular}:A'=AU

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solvability and parametrization of a single linear Diophantine equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes all integral solutions of one nonzero integral linear equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), and \(g=\gcd(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\). The equation \(ax=c\) has a solution \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) if and only if \(c\in\mathbb Z\) and \(g\mid c\). Moreover, there exists \(T\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) with \(T^{-1}\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}\) and \(aT=(g,0,\ldots,0)\); whenever the equation is solvable, its integral solutions are exactly \(x=T\binom{c/g}{z}\), where \(z\in\mathbb Z^{n-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonzero integral row vector a, ax=c has an integral solution exactly when c is an integer divisible by the gcd of the entries of a. An integral invertible change of coordinates reduces a to (g,0,...,0), and varying the remaining integer coordinates parametrizes every solution.

children.title: Reduced-Basis Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Basis Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lovász–Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász reduction with a general reduction parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\) be a basis of a lattice, let \(b_i^*\) be its Gram–Schmidt vectors, and put \(\mu_{i,j}=\langle b_i,b_j^*\rangle/\langle b_j^*,b_j^*\rangle\). For \(1/4<\delta<1\), the basis is \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced if
\[
|\mu_{i,j}|\le\tfrac12\quad(1\le j<i\le r)
\]
and
\[
\delta\|b_{i-1}^*\|^2\le\|b_i^*+\mu_{i,i-1}b_{i-1}^*\|^2\quad(2\le i\le r).
\]
This representation combines size reduction with the Lovász condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LLL-reduced lattice basis satisfies bounded Gram–Schmidt coefficients and the Lovász inequality, giving a geometrically controlled representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced exactly when the displayed size-reduction and Lovász inequalities hold.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced basis of a rank-\(r\) lattice \(L\).

notation.meaning: length of a shortest nonzero vector of L

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-vector quality guaranteed by LLL reduction.

source_refs.locator: 6.2 Basis reduction in lattices p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) have rank \(r\), and let \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_r)\) be a \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced basis with \(1/4<\delta<1\). Define \(\alpha=(\delta-1/4)^{-1}\), and let \(\lambda_1(L)=\min\{\|x\|:x\in L\setminus\{0\}\}\). Then
\[
\|b_1\|\le \alpha^{(r-1)/2}\lambda_1(L).
\]
In particular, for \(\delta=3/4\), the first basis vector satisfies \(\|b_1\|\le2^{(r-1)/2}\lambda_1(L)\), providing a dimension-dependent approximation to a shortest nonzero lattice vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first vector of an LLL-reduced rank-r basis approximates a shortest lattice vector within an explicit exponential factor.

children.title: Basis Encoding Size
children.top_down_role: Bit-size characteristics of lattice-basis representations.

assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb Z^{m\times r}\) has linearly independent columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle B\rangle=O(\langle m\rangle+\langle r\rangle+mr(1+\log_2(M+1)))\) for \(M=\max_{i,j}|b_{ij}|\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of a nonnegative integer k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary representation length of an integral lattice basis.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer basis matrix \(B=(b_{ij})\in\mathbb Z^{m\times r}\), let \(\langle k\rangle\) denote the binary encoding length of a nonnegative integer \(k\), and define the signed binary encoding length by
\[
\langle B\rangle=\langle m\rangle+\langle r\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{r}\bigl(1+\lceil\log_2(|b_{ij}|+1)\rceil\bigr).
\]
For \(M=\max_{i,j}|b_{ij}|\), this gives
\[
\langle B\rangle=O\bigl(\langle m\rangle+\langle r\rangle+mr(1+\log_2(M+1))\bigr),
\]
which is an input-size measure for bit-complexity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer basis is encoded by its dimensions, signs, and binary entries; its length is bounded by the dimension overhead plus the number of entries times one plus the logarithm of the largest entry magnitude.

children.title: Basis Conditioning Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation regimes where poor basis geometry degrades structural usability.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Conditioning Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unimodular equivalence does not control geometric conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each integer \(N\ge1\), let
\[
B_N=\begin{pmatrix}1&N\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Because \(\det(B_N)=1\), its columns form a basis of \(\mathbb Z^2\), just as the identity basis does. Nevertheless, its orthogonality defect is \(\|b_1\|\|b_2\|/|\det(B_N)|=\sqrt{N^2+1}\), and its spectral condition number satisfies \(\kappa_2(B_N)=\|B_N\|_2\|B_N^{-1}\|_2\ge N^2\). Hence fixed lattice determinant, unimodularity, and small dimension alone impose no uniform basis-conditioning bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unimodular shear bases of the same lattice can have arbitrarily large orthogonality defect and condition number.
assumptions_latex: Matrix conditioning is measured in the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_N\mathbb Z^2=\mathbb Z^2\) while \(\kappa_2(B_N)\to\infty\) and the orthogonality defect tends to infinity as \(N\to\infty\).
