knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary-Kernel Alternative Characterization of Total Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes total unimodularity by an alternative between row domination and inequalities tested on binary kernel vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be an integral matrix and \(D=[I\;-I\;A\;-A]\), where the blocks are horizontally concatenated and conformable. Then \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every conformable real vector \(w\), the following are equivalent: (i) there exists a real vector \(y\) such that \(yD\geq w\); (ii) \(wx\leq0\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\operatorname{cols}(D)}\) satisfying \(Dx=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix A is totally unimodular exactly when, for every vector w, domination of w by a row combination of the augmented matrix [I, -I, A, -A] is equivalent to w being nonpositive on every binary vector in that augmented matrix's kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff \forall w\;\Big[(\exists y:\ yD\geq w)\iff(\forall x\in\{0,1\}^{\operatorname{cols}(D)},\ Dx=0:\ wx\leq0)\Big].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Matroid and Matrix Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines representability of a matroid over a field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair (S,\mathcal I) is a linear matroid represented over a field \mathbb F if the elements of S are, or are represented by, the columns of a matrix A over \mathbb F and, for every T\subseteq S, T\in\mathcal I if and only if the corresponding columns of A are linearly independent. This construction satisfies the matroid axioms, and A is called a representation of (S,\mathcal I).

S\text{ is identified with or represented by the columns of }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall T\subseteq S,\quad T\in\mathcal I\iff A_T\text{ has linearly independent columns},\quad\text{and }(S,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Box-Constrained Feasibility Characterization of Total Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes total unimodularity by signed compatibility inequalities for bounded two-sided linear systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\). Then \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every \(a,b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(c,d\in\mathbb R^n\), the following are equivalent: (i) \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:c\leq x\leq d,\ a\leq Ax\leq b\}\neq\varnothing\); (ii) \(a\leq b\), \(c\leq d\), and for every \(u\in\{0,\pm1\}^m\) and \(v\in\{0,\pm1\}^n\) satisfying \(u^{\mathsf T}A=v^{\mathsf T}\), one has \(\sum_{i:v_i=-1}c_i+\sum_{j:u_j=1}a_j\leq\sum_{i:v_i=1}d_i+\sum_{j:u_j=-1}b_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix A is totally unimodular exactly when every bounded two-sided system involving A is feasible precisely when its componentwise bounds are ordered and every conformable signed ternary relation uA = v satisfies the stated compatibility inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff \forall a,b,c,d\;\Big[\exists x:\ c\leq x\leq d,\ a\leq Ax\leq b\iff a\leq b,\ c\leq d,\ \forall u,v\in\{0,\pm1\},\ u^{\mathsf T}A=v^{\mathsf T}:\ \sum_{i:v_i=-1}c_i+\sum_{j:u_j=1}a_j\leq\sum_{i:v_i=1}d_i+\sum_{j:u_j=-1}b_j\Big].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Chain Groups and Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines chain groups and regularity using support-contained decompositions, without imposing an unsupported sign-conformity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A chain group is a subgroup \(C\leq (\mathbb Z^n,+)\). It is regular if, for every \(x\in C\), there exist \(m\geq 1\) and \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\cap\{0,\pm1\}^n\) such that \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\) and \(\operatorname{supp}(x_i)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(x)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chain group is a subgroup of the integer lattice. It is regular when each of its vectors is a sum of ternary vectors from the group, each supported within the original vector's support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is regular}\iff \forall x\in C\;\exists m\geq1,\ x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\cap\{0,\pm1\}^n:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\ \land\ \forall i,\ \operatorname{supp}(x_i)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Integral-Attainment Characterization of Total Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes total unimodularity through integral attainment on both sides of a primal–dual linear-programming pair for every integral right-hand side and objective whenever the displayed optima are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\). Then \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\), whenever the two optima are finite,\[\max\{c^\top x:x\ge 0,\ Ax\le b\}=\min\{y^\top b:y\ge 0,\ A^\top y\ge c\}\]is attained by some \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\) on the primal side and some \(y\in\mathbb Z^m\) on the dual side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix A is totally unimodular if and only if, for every integral right-hand side b and integral objective c, both finite optima in the associated primal–dual linear-programming pair are attained by integral primal and dual vectors.
assumptions_latex: \max\{c^\top x:x\ge0,\ Ax\le b\}\text{ and }\min\{y^\top b:y\ge0,\ A^\top y\ge c\}\text{ are finite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff\text{ every such finite primal and dual optimum is attained by integral }x\text{ and }y.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular and let \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\). Then the rational polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) is integral. Equivalently, every nonempty face of \(P\) contains an integer point, and \[P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb Z^n)+\operatorname{rec}(P).\] In particular, whenever a linear objective has a finite optimum over \(P\), it has an integer optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A totally unimodular inequality matrix with an integer right-hand side defines an integral polyhedron; every finitely attained linear optimum has an integer optimizer.

Thus every vertex of \(Q\) is integral, and \[Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb Z^n)+\operatorname{rec}(Q).\] Consequently, if a linear objective attains a finite optimum over the nonempty set \(Q\), some integer point of \(Q\) is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A totally unimodular equality matrix, integer right-hand side, and nonnegative variables define an integral standard-form polyhedron.

assumptions_latex: \(b\) is integral whenever it is used as a right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([A\ I]\) and \(\begin{bmatrix}A\\-A\end{bmatrix}\) are totally unimodular, but lattice-changing substitutions need not preserve total unimodularity or integrality.

notation.meaning: Identity matrix of the required order

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Total Unimodularity p. 131

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\) is totally unimodular, then adjoining unit columns and duplicating rows with reversed sign preserve total unimodularity: \([A\ I]\) and \(\begin{bmatrix}A\\-A\end{bmatrix}\) are totally unimodular. Hence \(Ax\le b\) may be written as \(Ax+s=b\), \(s\ge0\), and \(Ax=b\) as two opposite inequalities without losing the certificate. Arbitrary substitutions need not preserve it: replacing \(x\) by \(2y\) changes \(x=1\) into \(2y=1\), whose coefficient matrix is not totally unimodular and whose solution is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slack variables and opposite inequalities preserve total unimodularity, but general substitutions can change the integer lattice and destroy both the certificate and integrality.
knowledge_statements.title: System-Form Conversion Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular. Appending lower and upper variable bounds gives the matrix \[\begin{bmatrix}A\\I\\-I\end{bmatrix},\] which is totally unimodular. Therefore, for \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\) and integral finite components of \(l,u\), the polyhedron \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ l\le x\le u\}\] is integral. Components having no finite bound are represented by omitting the corresponding unit row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Appending integral lower or upper variable bounds to a totally unimodular inequality system preserves total unimodularity and integrality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular, let \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and let \(J_+,J_-\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Define \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ x_j\ge 0\text{ for }j\in J_+,\ x_j\le 0\text{ for }j\in J_-\}.\] The constraint matrix obtained by appending the corresponding selected rows of \(I\) and \(-I\) to \(A\) is totally unimodular. Consequently, \(P\) is an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any specified collection of coordinatewise nonnegativity and nonpositivity restrictions can be appended to a totally unimodular inequality system without losing total unimodularity; with an integer right-hand side, the resulting polyhedron is integral.

children.title: Augmentation Preservation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on integrality preservation under bound or sign augmentation.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is an arbitrary proposed column-augmentation block with the same number of rows as \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total unimodularity of \(A\) alone does not imply total unimodularity of \([A\ C]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The preservation guarantee is limited to TU-compatible augmentations and does not extend to arbitrary new coefficient blocks.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Total Unimodularity p. 131

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Total unimodularity is not preserved under arbitrary column augmentation. For example, \(A=[1]\) is totally unimodular, but adjoining \(C=[2]\) gives \([A\ C]=[1\ 2]\), which is not totally unimodular. The associated standard-form polyhedron \[P=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R_+^2:x+2y=1\}\] has the fractional vertex \((0,\tfrac12)\). Thus total unimodularity of the original block alone supplies no preservation guarantee for an arbitrary augmenting block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary column augmentation can destroy total unimodularity; adjoining a coefficient equal to two already yields a non-TU matrix and a fractional standard-form vertex.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmentation Preservation Boundary

children.title: Data-Lattice Boundary
children.top_down_role: Dependence of TU-based integrality on the lattice of the system data.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The TU-defined polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R:Ax=b\}\) is not integral.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of right-hand-side lattice compatibility in TU-based integrality results.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Total Unimodularity p. 131

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Total unimodularity does not guarantee integrality when the right-hand side is outside the integer lattice. For \(A=[1]\) and \(b=\tfrac12\), the matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular, but \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R:Ax=b\}=\{\tfrac12\}\] has no integer point and is not an integral polyhedron. Thus the integral-right-hand-side hypothesis in the TU integrality theorem is substantive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A totally unimodular matrix can define a nonintegral polyhedron when the right-hand side is fractional; the one-variable equation x equals one half is already a counterexample.
knowledge_statements.title: Data-Lattice Boundary

children.title: Characterizations of Total Unimodularity
children.top_down_role: Equivalent determinant, signing, and combinatorial viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if it satisfies the stated row-signing condition.

notation.meaning: An arbitrary subset of row indices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ghouila-Houri signing characterization, equivalent to the determinant definition.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Total Unimodularity p. 131

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), the following are equivalent: every square subdeterminant of \(A\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\); and, for every subset \(R\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), there exist signs \(\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}\) for \(i\in R\) such that, for every column \(j\), \[\sum_{i\in R}\varepsilon_i a_{ij}\in\{-1,0,1\}.\] Hence the determinant definition and the Ghouila-Houri row-signing criterion characterize exactly the same matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer matrix is totally unimodular exactly when every row subset can be signed so each signed column sum is minus one, zero, or one.
knowledge_statements.title: Characterizations of Total Unimodularity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Signed-vector GCD characterization of total unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes total unimodularity through primitivity of every nonzero signed ternary row combination of every nonsingular submatrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every nonsingular \(r\times r\) submatrix \(B\) of \(A\) and every nonzero vector \(y\in\{0,\pm1\}^r\), the greatest common divisor of the entries of \(y^{\mathsf T}B\) is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is totally unimodular exactly when every nonzero 0, ±1 combination of the rows of every nonsingular submatrix has entries with greatest common divisor one.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is a nonsingular }r\times r\text{ submatrix of }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff\gcd\left((y^{\mathsf T}B)_1,\ldots,(y^{\mathsf T}B)_r\right)=1\text{ for every such }B,y.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of total unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Seven equivalent determinant, polyhedral-integrality, column-partition, parity, and divisibility conditions for a matrix with entries in \(\{0,\pm1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,\pm1\}^{m\times n}\). The following are equivalent: (i) every square submatrix of \(A\) has determinant in \(\{0,\pm1\}\); (ii) for every integral vector \(b\), the polyhedron \(\{x\mid x\geq0,\ Ax\leq b\}\) has only integral vertices; (iii) for all integral vectors \(a,b,c,d\), the polyhedron \(\{x\mid c\leq x\leq d,\ a\leq Ax\leq b\}\) has only integral vertices; (iv) every collection of columns of \(A\) can be partitioned into two parts such that the sum of the columns in one part minus the sum in the other has entries only in \(\{0,\pm1\}\); (v) every nonsingular submatrix of \(A\) has a row with an odd number of nonzero entries; (vi) the sum of all entries of any square submatrix having even row sums and even column sums is divisible by \(4\); (vii) no square submatrix of \(A\) has determinant \(2\) or \(-2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a matrix with entries 0, 1, or −1, total unimodularity is equivalent to six further conditions involving integral vertices, signed column partitions, odd row support, divisibility by four, and the exclusion of determinant ±2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conditions (i)--(vii) are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer-decomposition characterization of total unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An equivalence between total unimodularity and a uniform integer-decomposition property for nonnegative inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integral matrix \(A\) is totally unimodular if and only if, for every \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), every \(y\in\mathbb Z^n\), and every integer \(k\geq1\) satisfying \(y\geq0\) and \(Ay\leq kb\), there exist integral vectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\{x\mid x\geq0,\ Ax\leq b\}\) such that \(y=x_1+\cdots+x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix is totally unimodular exactly when every integral nonnegative vector feasible for a k-fold scaled right-hand side decomposes into k integral nonnegative vectors, each feasible for the original right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff\left(\forall b,y,k:\ y\geq0,\ Ay\leq kb\Rightarrow\exists x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb Z^n:\ x_i\geq0,\ Ax_i\leq b,\ y=\sum_{i=1}^k x_i\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matroid and Independent Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-axiom definition for finite matroids.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let E be a finite set and let \mathcal I\subseteq 2^E be nonempty. The pair (E,\mathcal I) is a matroid if (i) T\in\mathcal I and R\subseteq T imply R\in\mathcal I, and (ii) whenever T,U\in\mathcal I with |T|<|U|, there exists u\in U\setminus T such that T\cup\{u\}\in\mathcal I. The members of \mathcal I are called the independent sets of the matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matroid is a finite ground set together with a nonempty hereditary family of subsets satisfying the augmentation axiom; members of the family are its independent sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid exactly when the hereditary and augmentation axioms hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle-Sign Criterion for Total Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded criterion together with its stated column-incidence corollary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=(\alpha_{ij})\) be a \(\{0,\pm1\}\)-matrix. Suppose that, for every \(k\ge2\) and every alternating cycle \(\alpha_{i_1j_1},\alpha_{i_2j_1},\alpha_{i_2j_2},\ldots,\alpha_{i_kj_k},\alpha_{i_1j_k}\), the product of its entries belongs to \(\{(-1)^k,0\}\). Then \(A\) is totally unimodular. Consequently, every \(\{0,\pm1\}\)-matrix having exactly one \(+1\) and exactly one \(-1\) in each column is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A {0, ±1}-matrix is totally unimodular if every alternating cycle has entry product (-1)^k or zero. In particular, a {0, ±1}-matrix with exactly one +1 and one -1 in every column is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is totally unimodular; in particular, }\bigl[\forall j,\ |\{i:\alpha_{ij}=1\}|=|\{i:\alpha_{ij}=-1\}|=1\bigr]\Rightarrow A\text{ is totally unimodular}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed node–arc incidence matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and immediate structural properties for a digraph whose arcs have distinct endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph \(D=(V,A)\), with each arc \(e=uv\) having tail \(u\), head \(v\), and \(u\ne v\), the incidence matrix \(A_D=(a_{we})\in\{0,\pm1\}^{V\times A}\) is defined by \(a_{we}=-1\) if \(w=u\), \(a_{we}=1\) if \(w=v\), and \(a_{we}=0\) otherwise. Thus every column has exactly one \(-1\) and one \(+1\), so the rows sum to the zero vector and are linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed incidence matrix has one row per node and one column per arc, with −1 at the tail, +1 at the head, and zero elsewhere. Every column sums to zero, so the matrix rows sum to zero and are linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_{we}=\begin{cases}-1,&w=u,\\1,&w=v,\\0,&w\notin\{u,v\},\end{cases}\qquad \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}A_D=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Doubly stochastic and permutation matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the matrix classes used in the Birkhoff–von Neumann theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 1\), a matrix \(A=(\alpha_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is doubly stochastic if \(\alpha_{ij}\ge 0\) for all \(i,j\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\), and \(\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\). A permutation matrix is a matrix in \(\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\) with exactly one \(1\) in each row and each column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A doubly stochastic matrix is nonnegative and has every row sum and column sum equal to one. A permutation matrix is a zero-one square matrix with exactly one 1 in every row and column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is doubly stochastic}\iff\left(\alpha_{ij}\ge0\ \forall i,j,\ \sum_i\alpha_{ij}=1\ \forall j,\ \sum_j\alpha_{ij}=1\ \forall i\right);\quad A\text{ is a permutation matrix}\iff A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\text{ has exactly one }1\text{ in each row and column}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the Birkhoff polytope as the convex hull of permutation matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every regular matroid \(M\) can be constructed by repeated \(1\)-, \(2\)-, and \(3\)-sum operations from matroids that are graphic, cographic, or isomorphic to the exceptional ten-element regular matroid \(R_{10}\). Conversely, these basic matroids are regular and the three sum operations preserve regularity. Because regular matroids are precisely the matroids representable by totally unimodular matrices, this gives the structural decomposition underlying the general totally unimodular matrix class, up to standard representation operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every regular matroid decomposes through one-, two-, and three-sums into graphic, cographic, and exceptional R10 pieces, yielding the structural basis of general TU matrices.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists an algorithm which, given \(A\in\{-1,0,1\}^{m\times n}\), decides whether every square submatrix of \(A\) has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). The algorithm may use row and column permutations, sign changes, network-matrix recognition, and decomposition into regular-matroid components. Its number of arithmetic and combinatorial operations is bounded by a polynomial in \(m+n\); it either returns a decomposition certificate establishing total unimodularity or identifies a square submatrix whose determinant has absolute value at least \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total unimodularity is decidable in polynomial time, with either a structural decomposition certificate or a subdeterminant witnessing failure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Right-hand-side proximity of integer optima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directional infinity-norm sensitivity bound between optimal integer solutions for two right-hand sides and a common objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) have every subdeterminant bounded in absolute value by \(\Delta\), let \(b',b''\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(c\in\mathbb R^{1\times n}\). Suppose \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b',\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) and \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b'',\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) are finite. Then, for every optimal solution \(z'\) of the first problem, there exists an optimal solution \(z''\) of the second such that \(\|z'-z''\|_\infty\le n\Delta(\|b'-b''\|_\infty+2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two finite integer linear programs with the same objective and determinant-bounded integral constraint matrix but different right-hand sides, every optimum for the first has an optimum for the second within infinity-norm distance n Delta times the right-hand-side distance plus two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall z'\in\operatorname{argmax}\{cx:Ax\le b',\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\},\ \exists z''\in\operatorname{argmax}\{cx:Ax\le b'',\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}:\ \|z'-z''\|_\infty\le n\Delta\bigl(\|b'-b''\|_\infty+2\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Unimodularity Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines three local properties of an integral matrix–right-hand-side pair and states their hierarchy and connection to global unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) and \(h\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}\). Consider each column submatrix \(B\) of \(A\) that has full column rank and for which \(Bx=h\) has a solution \(x>0\). The pair \((A,h)\) is locally unimodular if every such \(B\) is unimodular; locally strongly unimodular if every such \(B\) contains a nonsingular submatrix of order \(\operatorname{rank}(B)\) having determinant \(\pm1\); and locally totally unimodular if every such \(B\) is totally unimodular. Local total unimodularity implies local strong unimodularity, which implies local unimodularity. Moreover, \(A\) is unimodular if and only if \((A,h)\) is locally unimodular for every integral vector \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integral matrix and integral right-hand side, inspect every full-column-rank column submatrix that represents the right-hand side using strictly positive coefficients. Requiring each such submatrix to be totally unimodular, to contain a full-rank determinant-±1 square submatrix, or merely to be unimodular gives a descending hierarchy. The matrix is globally unimodular exactly when it is locally unimodular for every integral right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (A,h)\text{ locally totally unimodular}\Rightarrow(A,h)\text{ locally strongly unimodular}\Rightarrow(A,h)\text{ locally unimodular},\qquad A\text{ unimodular}\iff \forall h\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\ (A,h)\text{ is locally unimodular}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform bounded integral representation of integer hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here the braces in the extracted display denote the integer hull of the indicated linear system, as required by the section context on facets of the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every rational matrix \(A\) there exists an integral matrix \(M\) such that, for every column vector \(b\) of compatible dimension, there exists a column vector \(d\) satisfying
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax\le b\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Mx\le d\}.
\]
If \(A\) is integral and every subdeterminant of \(A\) has absolute value at most \(\Delta\), then \(M\) may be chosen so that every entry satisfies \(|M_{ij}|\le n^{2n}\Delta^n\), where \(n\) is the number of columns of \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any rational constraint matrix A, one integral matrix M can be chosen uniformly for all compatible right-hand sides b so that each resulting integer hull is described by Mx ≤ d for a suitable d. If A is integral and all its subdeterminants are bounded in absolute value by Δ, the entries of M can be bounded by n^(2n)Δ^n, where n is the number of columns of A.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the quantitative bound: }A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\text{ and every subdeterminant of }A\text{ has absolute value at most }\Delta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M\in\mathbb Z^{r\times n}\ \forall b\in\mathbb R^m\ \exists d\in\mathbb R^r:\ \operatorname{conv}\{x\in\mathbb Z^n:Ax\le b\}=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Mx\le d\},\quad\text{with }|M_{ij}|\le n^{2n}\Delta^n\text{ in the bounded-subdeterminant case.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) of row rank \(m\) is unimodular if every nonsingular \(m\times m\) submatrix \(B\) obtained by selecting \(m\) columns of \(A\) satisfies \(\det(B)\in\{-1,1\}\). Thus unimodularity constrains only full-rank basis minors. It does not require arbitrary lower-order square minors to lie in \(\{-1,0,1\}\), which is the stronger total-unimodularity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-row-rank integer matrix is unimodular when every nonsingular basis submatrix has determinant plus or minus one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis-Defined Unimodularity and Identity Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines basis-dependent unimodularity and states its identity-augmentation connection with total unimodularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(U)=m\), a basis of \(U\) is a nonsingular \(m\times m\) submatrix. Such a matrix \(U\) is unimodular if it is integral and every basis \(B\) satisfies \(\det(B)\in\{-1,1\}\). Separately, for any \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\), \[A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff[I_p\ A]\text{ is unimodular}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank matrix, a basis is a nonsingular square submatrix containing one column for each row. The matrix is unimodular if it is integral and every basis has determinant 1 or -1. For any matrix A, A is totally unimodular exactly when its augmentation by the appropriate identity matrix is unimodular.
assumptions_latex: U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\ \operatorname{rank}(U)=m\text{ for the basis-defined notion}
A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\text{ for the identity-augmentation equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U\text{ is unimodular}\iff U\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\text{ and }\det(B)\in\{-1,1\}\text{ for every basis }B;\qquad A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff[I_p\ A]\text{ is unimodular}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unimodular matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines rectangular full-row-rank unimodularity through maximal minors and records the square-matrix specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(m\times n\) matrix \(A\) is unimodular if and only if it is integral, \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and every \(m\times m\) submatrix \(B\) satisfies \(\det(B)\in\{0,\pm1\}\). In particular, a square matrix \(U\) is unimodular if and only if it is integral and \(\det(U)=\pm1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix is unimodular when it is integral, has full row rank, and every maximal minor is zero or plus or minus one. For a square matrix, this is equivalent to integrality and determinant plus or minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is unimodular}\iff\left(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n},\ \operatorname{rank}(A)=m,\ \det(B)\in\{0,\pm1\}\text{ for every }m\times m\text{ submatrix }B\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Characterizations of Unimodular Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes unimodularity by integrality of two parameterized families of equality- and inequality-form polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(A\) is unimodular; (ii) for every \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}\), the polyhedron \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:x\geq 0,\ Ax=b\}\) is integral; (iii) for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\), the polyhedron \(\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{m}:yA\geq c\}\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix is unimodular exactly when every nonnegative equality system with an integral right-hand side defines an integral polyhedron, equivalently when every associated row-vector inequality system with an integral threshold vector defines an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is unimodular}\iff \forall b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\ \{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:x\geq0,\ Ax=b\}\text{ is integral}\iff \forall c\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\ \{y\in\mathbb{R}^{m}:yA\geq c\}\text{ is integral}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Unimodular Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent algebraic, inverse, lattice-preservation, and elementary-operation characterizations of square unimodular matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a nonsingular \(n\times n\) matrix. The following are equivalent: (i) \(U\) is unimodular; (ii) \(U\) and \(U^{-1}\) are integral; (iii) \(U^{-1}\) is unimodular; (iv) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(Ux\in\mathbb Z^n\) if and only if \(x\in\mathbb Z^n\); and (v) \(U\) is obtained from the identity matrix by a sequence of unimodular operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square nonsingular matrix, unimodularity is equivalent to integrality of the matrix and its inverse, unimodularity of the inverse, preservation and reflection of integer vectors, and construction from the identity by unimodular operations.
assumptions_latex: U\text{ is a nonsingular }n\times n\text{ matrix}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{(i)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(ii)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(iii)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(iv)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(v)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis-Factorization Characterization of Unimodularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes arbitrary-rank unimodularity through a unimodular column basis and a totally unimodular coordinate matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be an integral matrix. The following are equivalent: (i) \(A\) is unimodular; (ii) there exists a basis \(B\) of \(A\) such that \(B\) is unimodular and the unique matrix \(C\) satisfying \(BC=A\) is totally unimodular; (iii) every basis \(B\) of \(A\) is unimodular and the unique matrix \(C\) satisfying \(BC=A\) is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix is unimodular exactly when one—and equivalently every—column basis is unimodular and the unique matrix expressing all columns in that basis is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is unimodular}\iff \exists B\text{ a basis of }A:\ B\text{ is unimodular and the unique }C\text{ with }BC=A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff \forall B\text{ a basis of }A,\ B\text{ and its corresponding }C\text{ have these properties}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Primal-Dual Attainment Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes unimodularity of the transpose by integral primal and dual optimal solutions whenever the displayed dual pair has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\). Then \(A^{\top}\) is unimodular if and only if, for every \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\) for which the displayed primal-dual optimal value is finite, \[\max\{cx:Ax\leq b\}=\min\{yb:y\geq0,\ yA=c\}\] is attained by an integral vector \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\) and an integral vector \(y\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transpose of an integral matrix is unimodular exactly when every finite primal-dual optimum with integral objective and right-hand-side data has both an integral primal optimizer and an integral dual optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\top}\text{ is unimodular}\iff \forall b\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}\ \forall c\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\ \text{whenever the common optimum is finite, it is attained by some }x\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\text{ and }y\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unimodular Matrix of Arbitrary Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends unimodularity to integral matrices of arbitrary rank and records closure under taking column submatrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r\). The matrix \(A\) is unimodular if it is integral and, for every submatrix \(B\) consisting of \(r\) linearly independent columns of \(A\), the greatest common divisor of the determinants of all order-\(r\) submatrices of \(B\) is \(1\). This agrees with the nonsingular and full-row-rank definitions of unimodularity. Every column submatrix of a unimodular matrix is unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r matrix is unimodular when it is integral and, for every choice of r independent columns, the greatest common divisor of the resulting order-r minors is 1. This extends the earlier nonsingular and full-row-rank definitions, and every column submatrix of a unimodular matrix is again unimodular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is unimodular}\iff A\text{ is integral and }\forall B\text{ consisting of }r\text{ independent columns of }A,\ \gcd\{\det M:M\text{ is an order-}r\text{ submatrix of }B\}=1;\quad A\text{ unimodular}\Rightarrow A_{[:,J]}\text{ unimodular for every }J.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis-normalization equivalence for full-row-rank matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equates integrality under every basis normalization with total unimodularity under every basis normalization or under one basis normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) have full row rank. The following are equivalent: (i) for every basis \(B\) of \(A\), the matrix \(B^{-1}A\) is integral; (ii) for every basis \(B\) of \(A\), the matrix \(B^{-1}A\) is totally unimodular; (iii) there exists a basis \(B\) of \(A\) for which \(B^{-1}A\) is totally unimodular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank matrix, integrality of every basis-normalized matrix, total unimodularity of every basis-normalized matrix, and total unimodularity of at least one basis-normalized matrix are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ denotes a nonsingular basis submatrix of }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall B,\ B^{-1}A\text{ is integral}\right)\iff\left(\forall B,\ B^{-1}A\text{ is totally unimodular}\right)\iff\left(\exists B,\ B^{-1}A\text{ is totally unimodular}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is balanced if there is no square submatrix of odd order \(k\ge 3\) having exactly two entries equal to \(1\) in every row and exactly two entries equal to \(1\) in every column. Equivalently, no submatrix of \(A\) is the vertex-edge incidence matrix of an odd cycle after independent permutations of its rows and columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix is balanced when it contains no odd square submatrix having exactly two ones in every row and column.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual integral-optimum characterizations of balanced matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent covering and packing characterizations of balanced zero-one matrices through integral primal and dual optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$. The following are equivalent: (i) $M$ is balanced; (ii) for every $b\in\{0,1\}^m$ and $c\in\mathbb{Z}^n$, if the optima are finite, both $\min\{c^Tx\mid x\geq0,\;Mx\geq b\}$ and $\max\{y^Tb\mid y\geq0,\;y^TM\leq c^T\}$ have integral optimal solutions; (iii) for every $h\in\{1,\infty\}^m$ and $c\in\mathbb{Z}^n$, if the optima are finite, both $\max\{c^Tx\mid x\geq0,\;Mx\leq h\}$ and $\min\{y^Th\mid y\geq0,\;y^TM\geq c^T\}$ have integral optimal solutions. In (iii), $h_i=\infty$ makes the corresponding primal constraint void and requires $y_i=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a zero-one matrix, balancedness is equivalent either to the stated integral-optimum property for every finite covering primal-dual pair or to the corresponding property for every finite packing pair with right-hand-side entries equal to one or infinity. An infinite component removes its primal constraint and fixes the corresponding dual variable to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (i)\iff(ii)\iff(iii),\text{ with }h_i=\infty\text{ interpreted as a void primal constraint and }y_i=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and elementary closure properties of balanced zero-one matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}$ is balanced if it contains no square submatrix of odd order having exactly two entries equal to $1$ in every row and every column. Balanced matrices are closed under taking submatrices, transposition, and permutations of rows or columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-one matrix is balanced if it has no odd-order square submatrix with exactly two ones in every row and every column. Balancedness is preserved under submatrices, transposition, and row or column permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is balanced}\iff M\text{ has no odd-order square submatrix with exactly two 1s in each row and column};\quad \text{the class is closed under submatrices, transposition, and row/column permutations.}

children.title: Bounded-Subdeterminant Classes
children.top_down_role: Quantitative relaxations of total unimodularity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) belongs to the bounded-subdeterminant class with bound \(Delta\) exactly when \(Delta(A)leDelta\).
review_flags: A precise authoritative source locator for the class terminology is missing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative determinant bound over square submatrices of every order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer matrix \(Ain\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\), define \[Delta(A)=max{|det(B)|: Btext{ is a square submatrix of }A},\] where the empty maximum is taken as \(0\). For a fixed integer \(Deltage 0\), the bounded-subdeterminant class with parameter \(Delta\) consists of all such matrices satisfying \(Delta(A)leDelta\). The case \(Delta=1\) is precisely total unimodularity for integer matrices, while larger \(Delta\) measure a quantitative relaxation of that condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-subdeterminant class consists of integer matrices whose square minors all have absolute determinant at most a fixed parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Subdeterminant Classes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total Dual Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total dual integrality for rational inequality systems and records total unimodularity as a sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational system \(Ax\le b\) is totally dual integral (TDI) if, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) for which \(\min\{y^Tb:y\ge0,\ y^TA=c^T\}\) is finite, the minimum has an optimizer \(y\in\mathbb{Z}^m\). Moreover, if \(A\) is totally unimodular, then \(Ax\le b\) is TDI for every \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational inequality system is TDI when every finite dual problem associated with an integral objective has an integral optimal multiplier. A totally unimodular matrix produces a TDI system for every rational right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax\le b\text{ is TDI}\iff\forall c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\text{ with finite dual minimum},\ \operatorname*{argmin}\{y^Tb:y\ge0,\ y^TA=c^T\}\cap\mathbb{Z}^m\ne\varnothing;\quad A\text{ totally unimodular}\Rightarrow Ax\le b\text{ is TDI for every }b\in\mathbb{Q}^m

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal-integer criterion for scaling one TDI inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization for a minimal TDI system defining a full-dimensional polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Ax\le b,\ ax\le\beta\) be a minimal TDI system defining a full-dimensional polyhedron, with \(A\) and \(a\) integral. For every \(\alpha>0\), the system \(Ax\le b,\ (\alpha a)x\le\alpha\beta\) is TDI if and only if \(\alpha=1/k\) for some \(k\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a minimal, full-dimensional TDI description with integral row vectors, scaling one inequality by a positive factor preserves TDI exactly when that factor is the reciprocal of a natural number.
assumptions_latex: Ax\le b,\ ax\le\beta\text{ is a minimal TDI system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax\le b,\ (\alpha a)x\le\alpha\beta\text{ is TDI}\iff\exists k\in\mathbb N:\alpha=1/k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total dual 1/k-integrality and scaling characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines total dual \(1/k\)-integrality and records its polyhedral, scaling, and primal consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb N\). A system \(Ax\le b\) is totally dual \(1/k\)-integral if, for every \(c\in\mathbb Z^n\) for which \(\min\{yb:y\ge0,\ yA=c\}\) is finite, this minimum has an optimizer \(y\in(1/k)\mathbb Z^m\). It is totally dual \(1/k\)-integral if and only if \((k^{-1}A)x\le k^{-1}b\) is TDI. If additionally \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), then for every integral \(c\) for which \(\max\{cx:Ax\le b\}\) is finite, the maximum has an optimizer in \((1/k)\mathbb Z^n\). Moreover, for any polyhedron \(P\), every face of \(P\) contains a point of \((1/k)\mathbb Z^n\) if and only if every supporting hyperplane of \(P\) contains such a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system is totally dual 1/k-integral when each finite dual problem induced by an integral objective has an optimal dual vector on the 1/k lattice. This is equivalent to ordinary TDI after scaling the system by 1/k. With an integral right-hand side it yields a 1/k-integral primal optimum, and the associated face criterion is equivalent to the supporting-hyperplane criterion.
assumptions_latex: \min\{yb:y\ge0,\ yA=c\}\text{ is finite for the defining condition}
b\in\mathbb Z^m\text{ for the primal consequence}
P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a polyhedron for the face criterion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax\le b\text{ is totally dual }1/k\text{-integral}\iff(k^{-1}A)x\le k^{-1}b\text{ is TDI}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and uniqueness of integral TDI descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States general existence, full-dimensional uniqueness, and the exact role of integral right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every rational polyhedron $P$ there exists a TDI system $Ax\le b$ with $A$ integral and $P=\{x:Ax\le b\}$. Such a description can be chosen with $b$ integral if and only if $P$ is integral. If $P$ is full-dimensional, there exists a unique minimal TDI system $Ax\le b$ with $A$ integral defining $P$; for this unique system, $b$ is integral if and only if $P$ is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every rational polyhedron has an integral-coefficient TDI description, and its right-hand side can be chosen integral exactly when the polyhedron is integral. If the polyhedron is full-dimensional, its minimal integral-coefficient TDI description is unique, and that description has an integral right-hand side exactly when the polyhedron is integral.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a rational polyhedron}
P\text{ is full-dimensional for the uniqueness assertion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n},\ b:\ Ax\le b\text{ is TDI and }P=\{x:Ax\le b\};\quad \exists\text{ such a description with }b\in\mathbb Z^m\iff P\text{ is integral};\quad P\text{ full-dimensional}\Rightarrow\exists!\text{ minimal such system, whose }b\in\mathbb Z^m\iff P\text{ is integral}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds–Giles integer optimal-value criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-valued support optimization over a rational polyhedron yields integral primal optimizers; the stated dual-integrality result is its TDI corollary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\). If, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\}\) is an integer or \(+\infty\), then whenever this maximum is finite it is attained by some \(x^*\in\mathbb{Z}^n\). In particular, if \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\) and, for every integral \(c\) for which \(\min\{y^\top b:y\ge0,\ y^\top A=c^\top\}\) is finite, the dual minimum has an integral optimizer, then the corresponding primal maximum has an integral optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every integral objective has an integer or unbounded maximum over a rational polyhedron, each finite such maximum is attained at an integral point. Consequently, an integral right-hand side together with integral optimal dual solutions for all finite integral-objective dual problems guarantees integral primal optimizers.
assumptions_latex: \text{Corollary: }b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\text{ and every finite dual minimum associated with }c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\text{ has an integral optimizer}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\text{ with finite primal maximum},\ \exists x^*\in\mathbb{Z}^n:\ Ax^*\le b,\ c^\top x^*=\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b\};\quad \text{the stated dual-integrality hypotheses imply the same conclusion.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total dual integrality and its integral-polyhedron consequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a rational TDI inequality system together with the basic theorem for integral right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational system \(Ax\le b\) is totally dual integral (TDI) if, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) for which \(\min\{y^\top b:y\ge0,\ y^\top A=c^\top\}\) is finite, the minimum is attained by an integral vector \(y^*\). If \(Ax\le b\) is TDI and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), then \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is an integral polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimum arborescence min-max theorem and TDI formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The rooted-arborescence minimum-length problem, its rooted-cut packing dual, and the TDI property of the rooted-cut covering system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a directed graph with root $r$, let $\mathcal A_r$ and $\mathcal C_r$ denote its families of $r$-arborescences and $r$-cuts, and let $l\in\mathbb Z_+^A$. Then the minimum $l$-length of an $r$-arborescence equals the largest number of $r$-cuts, with repetition allowed, that can be packed so that each arc $a$ occurs at most $l(a)$ times. If $C$ has as rows the incidence vectors of all $r$-cuts, then $\min\{lx:x\ge0,\ Cx\ge\mathbf1\}=\max\{y\mathbf1:y\ge0,\ yC\le l\}$, with integral optimal solutions whenever the optima are finite. Moreover, the system $x\ge0,\ Cx\ge\mathbf1$ is totally dual integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integral arc lengths, the minimum length of a rooted arborescence equals the maximum number of rooted cuts, allowing repetitions, that respect the arc capacities given by those lengths. The corresponding cut-covering LP and cut-packing dual have integral optima when finite, and the covering system is totally dual integral.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a directed graph with root }r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{T\in\mathcal A_r}\sum_{a\in T}l(a)=\max\left\{t:\exists C_1,\ldots,C_t\in\mathcal C_r,\ \sum_{i=1}^t\mathbf1_{\{a\in C_i\}}\le l(a)\ \forall a\in A\right\},\qquad \{x\ge0:Cx\ge\mathbf1\}\text{ is TDI}.

knowledge_statements.title: Description Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional scaling counterexample distinguishing a system property from a polyhedral property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R\). The systems \(x\le 1,\ -x\le 0\) and \(2x\le 2,\ -x\le 0\) both describe \(P=[0,1]\). The first system is TDI. For the second system and the integral objective \(c=1\), the dual problem is \[\min\{2y_1:2y_1-y_2=1,\ y_1,y_2\ge 0\}.\] Its optimum is uniquely attained at \((y_1,y_2)=(1/2,0)\), with value \(1\), while every integral feasible dual solution has value at least \(2\). Thus the second description is not TDI even though it defines the same polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard and row-scaled descriptions of the interval from zero to one have different TDI status, showing that TDI is a property of the written inequality system.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A xle b\), indexed by a finite set \(I\), be a TDI description of \(P\). children.title: Canonical TDI Systems

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical TDI Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical normal-cone Hilbert-basis representation for full-dimensional rational polyhedra, unique up to row ordering after duplicate removal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N_P(F)=\{a\in\mathbb{R}^n:F\subseteq\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}a^Tx\}\). For every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\), let \(H_F\) be the unique minimal Hilbert basis of the pointed rational cone \(N_P(F)\), and let \(H(P)=\bigcup_F H_F\), with duplicate vectors removed. For each \(a\in H(P)\), set \(h(P)_a=\sup\{a^Tx:x\in P\}\). Then \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a^Tx\leq h(P)_a\text{ for every }a\in H(P)\},\] and the displayed system is TDI. After primitive normalization and duplicate removal, it is determined by \(P\) up to row ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional rational polyhedron, the primitive minimal Hilbert bases of all face normal cones, paired with their support values, form a TDI representation canonical up to row ordering.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty full-dimensional rational polyhedron.
For each nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\), the normal cone uses the maximization convention specified in the statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(P)x\leq h(P)\) is a TDI representation of \(P\), canonical up to row ordering after primitive normalization and duplicate removal.

notation.meaning: Normal cone of P at the face F under the maximization convention.
Unique minimal Hilbert basis of the pointed rational cone N_P(F).
Union of the face-normal-cone Hilbert bases with duplicate vectors removed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Chvátal–Gomory closure from an integral TDI description
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the closure by componentwise right-hand-side rounding and gives polyhedrality for rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}, where Ax\le b is TDI and A is integral. Then P'=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le\lfloor b\rfloor\}, where \lfloor b\rfloor is taken componentwise. Consequently, P' is a polyhedron for every rational polyhedron P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between irredundant facet descriptions and richer canonical TDI descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every row of an irredundant description of the full-dimensional polyhedron \(P\) defines a facet. Consequently, there is a bijection \(\pi\) between the rows of the two descriptions and positive scalars \(\lambda_i\) such that
\[(A'_{\pi(i)},b'_{\pi(i)})=\lambda_i(A_i,b_i).\]
If all facet normals are primitive integral vectors, corresponding normalized rows coincide. A canonical TDI description may nevertheless contain inequalities redundant for describing \(P\), because additional normal-cone Hilbert-basis vectors can be required for integral dual certificates; polyhedral irredundancy and TDI minimality are therefore distinct notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Irredundant descriptions have the same facet inequalities up to positive scaling, while a TDI description may need additional polyhedrally redundant inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Irredundant Representation Relations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniqueness of full-dimensional irredundant facet descriptions and the distinction from TDI minimality are plausible and fit the property container, but no inspectable source is cited.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard definition of box-total dual integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard rational-box definition, which includes stability under integral variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The system \(Ax\leq b\) is box-totally dual integral if, for every rational box \(\ell\leq x\leq u\), the augmented system
\[Ax\leq b,\qquad \ell\leq x\leq u\]
is totally dual integral after inequalities with infinite endpoints are omitted. Equivalently, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) whose maximum over the boxed polyhedron is finite, the dual of the corresponding linear program has an integral optimal multiplier vector. In particular, box-TDI implies preservation of TDI after imposing arbitrary integral lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system is box-TDI when adjoining any rational coordinate box preserves total dual integrality; integral variable bounds are a special case.
knowledge_statements.title: Box-Total Dual Integrality

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-rounding characterization of box-TDI systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes rational box-TDI systems by ordinary TDI together with the neighboring-integral-objective property on their feasible polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational system \(Ax\le b\) is box-TDI if and only if it is TDI and, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), there exists \(\widetilde c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) such that \(\lfloor c\rfloor\le \widetilde c\le \lceil c\rceil\) componentwise and every optimum solution of \(\max\{c^\top x\mid Ax\le b\}\) is also an optimum solution of \(\max\{\widetilde c^\top x\mid Ax\le b\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: TDI invariance under elimination using an integral equality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence after eliminating an integral multiple of an equality row from another inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be integral; let \(d,a_1,a_2\) be integral vectors; let \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb Z\); and let \(b,\beta_1,\beta_2\) be rational. For a scalar variable \(\eta\), the system \(Ax+d\eta\le b,\ a_1x+\varepsilon\eta\le\beta_1,\ a_2x+\eta=\beta_2\) is TDI if and only if \(Ax+d\eta\le b,\ (a_1-\varepsilon a_2)x\le\beta_1-\varepsilon\beta_2,\ a_2x+\eta=\beta_2\) is TDI. The same equivalence holds for box-TDI.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the displayed integral equality to eliminate the scalar variable from another inequality preserves TDI in both directions, with the same equivalence for box-TDI.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&Ax+d\eta\le b,\ a_1x+\varepsilon\eta\le\beta_1,\ a_2x+\eta=\beta_2\text{ is (box-)TDI}\\&\iff Ax+d\eta\le b,\ (a_1-\varepsilon a_2)x\le\beta_1-\varepsilon\beta_2,\ a_2x+\eta=\beta_2\text{ is (box-)TDI}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed system \(Ax\leq b,\ A_Ix=b_I\) is TDI when equality multipliers are allowed to be integral and unrestricted in sign.

notation.meaning: Face obtained by making the indexed original inequalities tight.
Submatrix and subvector indexed by I.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: facial restriction of a TDI system by tight original rows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction to a face exposed by inequalities already present in the TDI system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Regard the face \(F\) as represented by
\[Ax\leq b,\qquad A_Ix=b_I.\]
For each integral objective \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) having a finite maximum on \(F\), the dual admits an optimum whose multipliers on \(Ax\leq b\) are nonnegative integers and whose multipliers on \(A_Ix=b_I\) are unrestricted integers. Thus facial restriction by setting original inequalities tight preserves total dual integrality under the mixed inequality-equality convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face obtained by making selected original TDI inequalities tight retains integral dual certificates when the new equality multipliers are unrestricted integers.
knowledge_statements.title: Facial Restrictions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact preservation claim depends on the mixed inequality-equality definition of TDI and on integral unrestricted equality multipliers. No source supports that convention or theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facewise Hilbert-Basis Characterization of TDI Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes total dual integrality by the active constraint rows on every face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Ax\le b be a rational system and let P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}. Then Ax\le b is totally dual integral if and only if, for every face F of P, the rows of A active on F form a Hilbert basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational inequality system is totally dual integral exactly when the constraint rows active on every face of its polyhedron form a Hilbert basis.
assumptions_latex: Ax\le b\text{ is a rational system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax\le b\text{ is TDI}\iff\forall F\unlhd P,\ \{a_i:a_i^Tx=b_i\text{ for every }x\in F\}\text{ forms a Hilbert basis.}

children.title: Bound Restrictions
children.top_down_role: TDI behavior after adding variable bounds or related restrictions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\leq b,\ \ell\leq x\leq u\) is TDI.

notation.meaning: Componentwise bounds; inequalities with infinite endpoints are omitted.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate defining preservation property of box-TDI
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-bound restriction under the box-TDI hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Intersect the feasible region with the coordinate box \([\ell,u]\). By box-total dual integrality, the augmented system
\[Ax\leq b,\qquad -x\leq-\ell,\qquad x\leq u\]
is TDI after omitting inequalities associated with infinite endpoints. Hence every integral objective with finite optimum over the restricted polyhedron has an optimal dual solution integral in the original-row, lower-bound, and upper-bound multipliers. No integrality of the finite bounds is needed for this dual-integrality conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Box-TDI systems remain TDI after any rational coordinate bounds are imposed, with integral optimal multipliers for both original rows and bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound Restrictions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is the defining preservation property of box-TDI and fits the property container, but no authoritative source with a locator is supplied.

children.title: Restriction Preservation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on TDI preservation across restricted systems.

assumptions_latex: TDI is interpreted as a property of a displayed inequality system, not solely of its feasible polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary TDI need not survive integral coordinate bounds; box-TDI is the corresponding uniform preservation condition.

notation.meaning: An integral triangle used to exhibit the restriction mechanism.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integral polyhedra admit TDI descriptions and integral-right-hand-side TDI systems define integral polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between ordinary TDI and preservation under coordinate bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The integral polygon \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(2,1),(0,2)\}\) admits an integral-right-hand-side TDI description. However,
\[P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:x_1\leq1\}\]
has fractional vertices \((1,\tfrac12)\) and \((1,\tfrac32)\). Therefore the system obtained by adjoining the integral bound \(x_1\leq1\) cannot be TDI with integral right-hand side, since such a system would define an integral polyhedron. Ordinary TDI thus does not guarantee bound-restriction preservation; requiring preservation for every box is precisely the stronger box-TDI condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral coordinate cut can create fractional vertices, so ordinary TDI may fail after a bound is added; box-TDI excludes this failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Restriction Preservation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate cut has the stated fractional vertices, but the argument also relies on the uncited theorem that the integral polygon admits an integral-right-hand-side TDI description.

children.title: TDI Cross-Space Transformation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Dual-integrality behavior across original and extended spaces.

children.title: Projected TDI Systems
children.top_down_role: TDI behavior after eliminating variables from a formulation.

assumptions_latex: \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+p}:Bx+Cy\leq d\}\) is represented by a TDI system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A displayed system \(Ax\leq b\) is a projected TDI system for \(Q\) only when it represents \(P\) and is itself TDI.

notation.meaning: Polyhedron in original and auxiliary variables.
Coordinate projection of Q onto x-space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: representation-sensitive definition of projected TDI system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-level notion; projection of a TDI polyhedron does not specify projected inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite inequality system \(Ax\leq b\) in the original variables is called a projected TDI system associated with \(Q\) when
\[\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\]
and \(Ax\leq b\) is TDI. The TDI property of \(Bx+Cy\leq d\) alone establishes neither condition for an arbitrary inequality list produced by elimination: exact projection must be verified, and the resulting rows must separately satisfy the integral-dual certificate condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected TDI system must exactly describe the projection and must itself be TDI; neither property follows for an arbitrary elimination output.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected TDI Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation-sensitive definition is internally coherent and fits the definition container, but “projected TDI system” and the associated projection warning require an authoritative source.

children.title: Extended TDI Formulations
children.top_down_role: TDI descriptions in spaces containing auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Bx+Cy\leq d\) is an extended TDI formulation of \(P\) exactly when it is TDI and \(P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\).

notation.meaning: Extended feasible region in original and auxiliary variables.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: extended formulation definition combined with TDI representation property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended formulations whose displayed lifted inequality system is TDI.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The system
\[Bx+Cy\leq d\]
is an extended TDI formulation of \(P\) if its feasible set \(Q\) is TDI as displayed and
\[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ Bx+Cy\leq d\}.\]
Thus the auxiliary variables may change the dual certificate space, but eliminating them must recover exactly \(P\). If \(d\) is integral, TDI implies that \(Q\) is integral; consequently its coordinate projection \(P\) is also an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended TDI formulation is a TDI lifted system whose projection is exactly the original polyhedron; an integral right-hand side also yields an integral projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended TDI Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed definition and integral-projection consequence are mathematically plausible and appropriately classified, but no source supports the terminology or claims.

children.title: Cross-Space Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of dual integrality when moving between original and extended spaces.

assumptions_latex: TDI is interpreted for the displayed system after changing variable space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection preserves the represented set but does not make every projected inequality representation TDI.

notation.meaning: A TDI extended polyhedron used in the counterexample.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: total unimodularity of the example and representation sensitivity of TDI
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of TDI transfer to arbitrary representations after projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The matrix of
\[Q=\{(x,y):x-y\leq0,\ y\leq1\}
\]
is totally unimodular, so the displayed extended system is TDI. Its projection onto the \(x\)-space is \(P=\{x:x\leq1\}\). For any integer \(k\geq2\), the equivalent projected description \(kx\leq k\) is not TDI: maximizing the integral objective \(x\) has the unique dual multiplier \(1/k\). Hence TDI in an extended space does not transfer to every system describing the projection; row normalization or a new TDI construction is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A TDI lift may project to a set represented by non-TDI inequalities; scaling the projected inequality already supplies a one-dimensional counterexample.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Space Failure Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly distinguishes a TDI lifted system from a non-TDI scaled representation of its projection and fits the failure-boundary container, but it has no citation.

children.title: TDI Reformulation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of TDI to coefficient changes and reformulation.

children.title: Coefficient Scaling
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of TDI descriptions to row or coefficient scaling.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(x\leq1\) by \(kx\leq k\) preserves the feasible set but destroys TDI.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive non-unimodular scaling of an inequality row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The system \(x\leq1\) is TDI: for every integral objective with finite maximum, its dual has an integral optimum. Multiplying its sole inequality by \(k\geq2\) produces the equivalent system
\[kx\leq k.\]
For the integral objective \(c=1\), the dual equation is \(ky=1\) with \(y\geq0\), so the only feasible and optimal multiplier is \(y=1/k\), which is not integral. Thus positive scaling preserves the polyhedron but need not preserve total dual integrality; primitive row normalization is mathematically substantive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling the TDI inequality x ≤ 1 by an integer k ≥ 2 leaves the feasible set unchanged but forces a fractional dual multiplier.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Scaling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-dimensional scaling counterexample is precise and correctly classified as a counterexample, but the required inspectable source is absent.

children.title: Constraint Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of TDI descriptions to combining constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(\lambda\in\mathbb{Z}_+^m\) and \(\lambda^TAx\leq\lambda^Tb\) is appended without deleting original rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Appending the aggregate preserves TDI, whereas replacing its constituent rows by the aggregate has no general preservation guarantee.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: zero multiplier extends every original integral dual certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes redundant augmentation from row replacement by an aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The aggregate \(\lambda^TAx\leq\lambda^Tb\) is valid for \(Ax\leq b\). When it is merely appended, the feasible set is unchanged, and every integral optimal dual certificate for the original system extends to the augmented dual by assigning multiplier zero to the new row. Therefore the augmented system remains TDI. If some original inequalities are deleted and replaced by their aggregate, this extension argument disappears: the feasible set may enlarge, and even when equivalence is restored by other rows, integral dual representability must be checked anew.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Appending a redundant aggregate preserves TDI because its dual multiplier can be zero; replacing original constraints by an aggregate need not preserve anything.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Aggregation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Appending the redundant aggregate preserves existing integral dual certificates, while replacement lacks a general guarantee. The property fits the container but has no cited source.

children.title: Reformulation Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Coefficient transformations that destroy total dual integrality.

assumptions_latex: \(M\geq0\) is used to form the reformulated system \(MAx\leq Mb\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible-set equivalence alone does not imply that \(MAx\leq Mb\) is TDI.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: TDI depends on the integral semigroup generated by active rows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary for preserving TDI under nonnegative row reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Nonnegative row transformation guarantees only \(P\subseteq P_M\), where
\[P=\{x:Ax\leq b\},\qquad P_M=\{x:MAx\leq Mb\}.\]
Even if additional structure gives \(P=P_M\), TDI can fail because \(M\) may change the integer semigroup generated by rows active on a face. The one-row choice \(A=(1)\), \(b=1\), and \(M=(k)\) with \(k\geq2\) yields the equivalent system \(kx\leq k\), whose dual multiplier for objective \(c=1\) is \(1/k\). Preservation therefore requires certificate-compatible transformations, not merely equivalent feasible regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative row reformulations may enlarge the set or alter active-row integer semigroups; even equivalent reformulations can lose TDI through nonprimitive scaling.
knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Failure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling example supports the stated failure boundary for equivalent nonnegative row reformulations, but no authoritative transformation or TDI source is cited.

notation.meaning: The polyhedron defined by the system.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) denote row \(i\) of \(A\), and for each nonempty face \(F\) define \(I(F)=\{i:a_i^{\mathsf T}x=b_i\text{ for every }x\in F\}\). children.title: TDI System Construction
children.top_down_role: Construction of TDI descriptions for integral polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist rational \(A,b\) with \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) such that \(Ax\le b\) is TDI; if \(P\) is integral, \(b\) may be chosen integral.

notation.meaning: The rational polyhedron to be represented.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of TDI descriptions, including the integral right-hand-side refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every rational polyhedron \(P\) admits a finite inequality description \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) that is totally dual integral. Such a description may be constructed by choosing, for each relevant normal cone, integral inequality normals forming a Hilbert basis and assigning their valid support values on \(P\). Moreover, when \(P\) is integral, the construction can be chosen with \(A\) rational and \(b\) integral. Consequently, integrality of \(P\) is equivalent to the existence of a TDI description having an integral right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every rational polyhedron has a TDI inequality description. An integral rational polyhedron has one whose right-hand side is integral.
knowledge_statements.title: TDI System Construction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existence and integral-right-hand-side claims fit TDI System Construction, but the construction theorem and its refinement require an authoritative locator.

children.title: TDI Certificate Complexity
children.top_down_role: Representation-size issues for evidence supporting recognition or construction.

assumptions_latex: The rational data \((A,b)\) are represented in binary.
The decision problem asks whether \(Ax\le b\) is TDI.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: TDI recognition is coNP-complete, while failure of TDI admits a polynomially checkable certificate of polynomial encoding length.

notation.meaning: The binary encoding length of the input system.
A face of the polyhedron defined by the system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-encoding complexity of deciding TDI for rational inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under binary encoding of rational matrices and vectors, the decision problem \(\{(A,b):Ax\le b\text{ is TDI}\}\) is coNP-complete. A negative instance has a certificate of length polynomial in \(L(A,b)\): it identifies a nonempty face \(F\) and an integral vector in the cone generated by the rows active on \(F\) that is not a nonnegative integral combination of those rows. Verification consists of rational linear feasibility and integer-cone nonmembership checks encoded with polynomial-size auxiliary data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recognizing TDI systems is coNP-complete under binary encoding; non-TDI behavior has a polynomial-size certificate based on a face whose active normals fail the Hilbert-basis condition.
knowledge_statements.title: TDI Certificate Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind fits the leaf, but coNP-completeness and the claimed polynomial certificate—especially integer-cone nonmembership verification—require a precise complexity-theorem source.

children.title: Hilbert Bases of Rational Cones
children.top_down_role: Finite integer generating systems for rational cone lattices.

assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a lattice containing generators of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite set \(H\subseteq C\cap L\) is a Hilbert basis exactly when \(C\cap L=\mathbb{N}H\).

notation.meaning: The additive monoid of nonnegative integral combinations of \(H\).
The lattice points contained in the cone.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert bases relative to a specified ambient lattice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite set \(H=\{h_1,\ldots,h_t\}\subseteq C\cap L\) is a Hilbert basis of \(C\) relative to \(L\) if every lattice point of \(C\) is a nonnegative integral combination of its elements:
\[C\cap L=\mathbb{N}H:=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^t\lambda_jh_j:\lambda_j\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\right\}.\]
For a rational polyhedral cone, such a finite set exists. The lattice must be specified, since changing \(L\) changes both the lattice points to be generated and potentially the Hilbert basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hilbert basis is a finite set of lattice points whose nonnegative integer combinations produce every lattice point in a rational cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert Bases of Rational Cones

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lattice-relative definition is precise and appropriate, but the included finite-existence assertion for rational cones needs an inspectable Hilbert-basis or Gordan-lemma citation.

Every rational cone admits a Hilbert basis. A smallest Hilbert basis may be exponentially large relative to a generating set of the cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Hilbert and integral Hilbert bases and records existence and pointed-cone uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite set $H=\{a_1,\ldots,a_t\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is a Hilbert basis if every $b\in\operatorname{cone}(H)\cap\mathbb Z^n$ can be written as $b=\sum_{i=1}^t\lambda_i a_i$ with $\lambda_i\in\mathbb Z_+$. children.title: Affine-Semigroup Normality
children.top_down_role: Normal generation behavior of affine semigroups associated with rational cones.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq L\) is a finitely generated affine semigroup in a lattice \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is normal exactly when \(kx\in S\), \(x\in\operatorname{gp}(S)\), and \(k\ge1\) imply \(x\in S\).
