knowledge_statements.title: Generalization Strength Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficientwise strength comparison and incomparability among gauge cuts from different forbidden-set-free regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For closed convex sets \(B_1,B_2\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) containing \(f\) in their interiors, let \(C_i:=B_i-f\). If \(B_1\subseteq B_2\), then
\[
\gamma_{C_1}(r)\ge\gamma_{C_2}(r)
\quad\text{for every }r\in\mathbb R^q.
\]
Because cuts have the form \(\sum_j\gamma_{C_i}(r^j)s_j\ge1\) with \(s\ge0\), the cut from \(B_2\) dominates the cut from \(B_1\). For nonnested sets, if rays \(r^a,r^b\) satisfy opposite strict coefficient inequalities, neither cut dominates coefficientwise; this crossing is a structural strength gap between the generalizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger admissible convex regions yield stronger gauge cuts; nonnested regions can produce crossing ray coefficients and mutually incomparable cuts.
assumptions_latex: Both sets satisfy the required forbidden-set-free condition
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_1\subseteq B_2\Longrightarrow\gamma_{B_1-f}\ge\gamma_{B_2-f}\), while crossing coefficients preclude coefficientwise dominance.

notation.meaning: Translation of comparison region i to the origin.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: gauge antitonicity under set inclusion gives the stated cut-strength order
source needed to confirm that coefficientwise incomparability is the intended strength-gap notion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind fits a strength-gap leaf. Gauge antitonicity gives the stated dominance direction for inequalities of the form shown, and crossing coefficients preclude coefficientwise dominance, but no source confirms that coefficientwise incomparability is the intended strength-gap notion in this taxonomy.

children.title: Cut Dominance

knowledge_statements.title: Cut Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance of equally normalized intersection cuts relative to a common relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(C_i=\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\ge 1\}\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\) be valid cut halfspaces for the intended feasible set. Cut \(C_1\) dominates \(C_2\) relative to \(Q\) precisely when \[Q\cap C_1\subseteq Q\cap C_2.\] Equivalently, every point of \(Q\) satisfying \(a_1^{\mathsf T}x\ge1\) also satisfies \(a_2^{\mathsf T}x\ge1\). Equality of the two intersections gives equivalence; strict inclusion gives strict dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized cut dominates another when imposing the first on the common relaxation automatically enforces the second; strict containment means strict dominance.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the common comparison relaxation.
Both inequalities are valid and normalized to right-hand side \(1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\succeq_Q C_2\iff Q\cap C_1\subseteq Q\cap C_2\).

notation.meaning: common relaxation on which cuts are compared
halfspace induced by normalized cut i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative-containment definition is mathematically coherent and fits the Cut Dominance leaf, but the record supplies no citation or inspectable locator supporting this convention.

children.top_down_role: Quantitative criteria for comparing lattice-free cuts.

The scaling explanation was replaced by the precise geometric interpretation appropriate to the normalized inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise violation and Euclidean efficacy for normalized cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\bar x\in Q\), and consider the normalized cut \(a^{\mathsf T}x\ge 1\), where \(a\ne 0\). Define its violation and Euclidean efficacy at \(\bar x\) by \[v(a;\bar x)=\max\{0,1-a^{\mathsf T}\bar x\},\qquad e_2(a;\bar x)=\frac{v(a;\bar x)}{\lVert a\rVert_2}.\] If \(\bar x\) violates the cut, then \(e_2(a;\bar x)\) is the Euclidean distance from \(\bar x\) to the boundary hyperplane \(a^{\mathsf T}x=1\). These pointwise measures need not reproduce the dominance order, which compares cut halfspaces throughout a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Violation is the cut deficit at a test point, and efficacy is that deficit divided by the coefficient norm. At a violating point, efficacy equals the Euclidean distance to the cut boundary. Such local scores need not agree with global dominance.

children.title: Incomparability Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Incomparability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of either relative-dominance relation between two cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and let \(C_1,C_2\) be valid cut halfspaces. The cuts are incomparable relative to \(Q\) exactly when neither dominates the other: \[Q\cap C_1\nsubseteq Q\cap C_2\quad\text{and}\quad Q\cap C_2\nsubseteq Q\cap C_1.\] Equivalently, there exist witnesses \(x^{(1)},x^{(2)}\in Q\) such that \(x^{(1)}\in C_1\setminus C_2\) and \(x^{(2)}\in C_2\setminus C_1\). Thus each cut excludes a relaxation point admitted by the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two cuts are incomparable when each admits some relaxation point rejected by the other, so neither cut halfspace contains the other relative to the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are compared on the same relaxation \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_1\parallel_Q C_2\iff (Q\cap C_1\nsubseteq Q\cap C_2)\land(Q\cap C_2\nsubseteq Q\cap C_1)\).

notation.meaning: the cuts are incomparable relative to Q
witness point for failure of one containment

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice-Free Cut Closures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure obtained by intersecting all cuts generated from a prescribed lattice-free family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(S\) be the intended mixed-integer feasible set, and let \(\mathcal L\) be a prescribed family of lattice-free convex sets. For each \(L\in\mathcal L\), let \(\mathcal C(L,Q)\) denote the intersection-cut halfspaces obtained from \(L\) and valid for \(S\). The \(\mathcal L\)-lattice-free cut closure is \[\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal L}(Q)=Q\cap\bigcap_{L\in\mathcal L}\ \bigcap_{C\in\mathcal C(L,Q)}C.\] Consequently, \(S\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal L}(Q)\subseteq Q\), provided every generated halfspace is valid for \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lattice-free closure is the original relaxation intersected with every valid intersection-cut halfspace generated by sets in the prescribed lattice-free family.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal C(L,Q)\) is valid for \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_{\mathcal L}(Q)\subseteq Q\).

knowledge_statements.title: Valid Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity in the pure infinite-group relaxation over an abelian group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an abelian group, let \(f\in G\setminus\{0\}\), and define \(R_f(G)\) as the set of finitely supported functions \(y:G\to\mathbb Z_+\) satisfying \(\sum_{r\in G}r\,y(r)=f\) in \(G\). A function \(\pi:G\to\mathbb R_+\) is valid for this group relaxation when \[\sum_{r\in G}\pi(r)y(r)\ge1\qquad\text{for every }y\in R_f(G).\] The sum is finite because each feasible \(y\) has finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative function is valid when its coefficient sum is at least one for every finitely supported nonnegative integer combination representing the group element f.
assumptions_latex: Feasible multiplicity functions have finite support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ is valid}\iff \sum_{r\in G}\pi(r)y(r)\ge1\text{ for all }y\in R_f(G)\).

notation.meaning: pure group relaxation with right-hand side f
finitely supported nonnegative integer multiplicity function

children.title: Minimal Functions
children.top_down_role: Valid generators that are nondominated within the relevant ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise minimality among normalized valid functions for one group relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(R_f(G)\). A valid function \(\pi:G\to\mathbb R_+\) is minimal when no distinct valid function lies pointwise below it. Formally, \[\bigl(\pi'\text{ valid and }\pi'(r)\le\pi(r)\text{ for every }r\in G\bigr)\Longrightarrow \pi'=\pi.\] Equivalently, decreasing the coefficients of \(\pi\) in any nonzero pointwise direction destroys validity. Minimality is therefore an order notion and does not by itself assert extremality in the convex set of valid functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid function is minimal if no different valid function has coefficients everywhere no larger. This order property is distinct from convex extremality.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is valid for the fixed relaxation \(R_f(G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ is minimal}\iff [\pi'\le\pi\text{ and }\pi'\text{ valid}]\Rightarrow\pi'=\pi\).
review_flags: No supplied source locator covers minimal valid functions for group relaxations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formal pointwise-order definition fits Minimal Functions. The informal claim about decreasing coefficients should be read only for decreases that remain in the admissible nonnegative function class, and a source is required for the intended convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lattice-free gauge characterization of minimal valid functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal valid functions for the infinite relaxation \(R_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(\psi\) is a minimal valid function for \(R_f\) if and only if there exists a maximal \(\mathbb{Z}^q\)-free convex set \(B\) such that \(\psi\) is the gauge of \(B-f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function ψ is minimally valid for R_f exactly when it is the gauge of B−f for some maximal integer-lattice-free convex set B.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi\text{ is minimal valid for }R_f\iff \exists B\text{ maximal, convex, and }\mathbb{Z}^q\text{-free such that }\psi=\gamma_{B-f}.

knowledge_statements.title: Validity–Minimality Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domination reduction for nonnegative valid functions in the pure group model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an abelian group, let \(f\in G\setminus\{0\}\), and let \(\pi:G\to\mathbb R_+\) be valid for \(R_f(G)\). Under the standard domination theorem for the pure group relaxation, there exists a minimal valid function \(\bar\pi:G\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \[\bar\pi(r)\le\pi(r)\qquad\text{for every }r\in G.\] Hence the inequality generated by \(\bar\pi\) dominates the inequality generated by \(\pi\), and validity analysis may be reduced to minimal valid functions without losing undominated inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative valid group function is pointwise dominated by a minimal valid function, so undominated inequalities can be studied through minimal functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex extremality within the normalized valid-function set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(R_f(G)\), and let \(\mathcal V_f(G)\) be its convex set of nonnegative valid functions. A function \(\pi\in\mathcal V_f(G)\) is extreme when, for any \(\pi_1,\pi_2\in\mathcal V_f(G)\), \[\pi=\tfrac12(\pi_1+\pi_2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\pi_1=\pi_2=\pi.\] Equivalently, \(\pi\) is not the midpoint of two distinct valid functions. This definition concerns convex decomposition, rather than pointwise domination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme valid function cannot be expressed as the midpoint of two distinct valid functions in the same normalized group model.
assumptions_latex: All functions belong to the same normalized valid-function set \(\mathcal V_f(G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ is extreme}\iff [\pi=(\pi_1+\pi_2)/2]\Rightarrow\pi_1=\pi_2=\pi\).

notation.meaning: convex set of nonnegative valid functions for the fixed group relaxation

knowledge_statements.title: Facet Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional facet definition through containment of tight feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid function \(\pi\), define its tight set by \[P(\pi)=\left\{y\in R_f(G):\sum_{r\in G}\pi(r)y(r)=1\right\}.\] A valid function \(\pi\) is a facet function when, for every valid function \(\pi'\), \[P(\pi)\subseteq P(\pi')\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\pi'=\pi.\] Thus the feasible group solutions made tight by \(\pi\) uniquely determine the normalized valid function among all valid functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A facet function is uniquely determined among valid functions by its tight feasible group solutions: any valid function tight on all of them must coincide with it.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) and \(\pi'\) use the same right-hand-side normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ is a facet}\iff P(\pi)\subseteq P(\pi')\Rightarrow\pi'=\pi\text{ for every valid }\pi'\).

notation.meaning: feasible group solutions satisfying the inequality of pi at equality

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the tight-set definition of a facet function.
The intended finite- or infinite-group facet convention should be source-checked.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tight-set predicate is coherent and fits Facet Functions, but facet conventions can differ between finite and infinite group models. A precise source is required to establish that this is the intended functional facet definition and to identify the comparison class for \(\pi'\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet Theorem for a Minimal Valid Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a uniqueness-based sufficient condition for a minimal valid function to define a facet of the infinite-group relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi\) be a minimal valid function. If the set of equalities \(E(\pi)\) has no solution other than \(\pi\), then \(\pi\) defines a facet of \(G_f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If π is a minimal valid function and π is the unique solution of the equalities E(π), then π defines a facet of G_f.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ defines a facet of }G_f.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet Function for the Infinite Group Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines facet status for a valid function by maximality of its equality-contact set with the infinite-group relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a valid function \(\pi\), define \[P(\pi):=\left\{x\in G_f:\sum_{r\in\mathbb{O}^q}\pi(r)x_r=1\right\}.\] Then \(\pi\) defines a facet of \(G_f\) if and only if there is no other valid function \(\pi^*\neq\pi\) such that \(P(\pi)\subseteq P(\pi^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a valid function π, let P(π) be the points of G_f satisfying its valid inequality at equality. The function π defines a facet when no distinct valid function π* has an equality-contact set containing P(π).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ defines a facet of }G_f\iff\nexists\text{ valid }\pi^*\neq\pi\text{ with }P(\pi)\subseteq P(\pi^*)\).

children.title: Extremality–Facet Distinctions
children.top_down_role: Coincidence, implication, and separation regimes for the two notions.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremality–Facet Distinctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical distinction between convex indecomposability and tight-set uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a fixed normalized group relaxation, extremality and facetness impose different predicates. Extremality excludes a nontrivial identity \(\pi=\tfrac12(\pi_1+\pi_2)\) with valid \(\pi_1\ne\pi_2\); facetness requires \(P(\pi)\subseteq P(\pi')\) to force \(\pi'=
\pi\) for every valid \(\pi'\). Under the standard functional facet theorem, every facet function is extreme. The converse is model-dependent and must not be asserted without additional hypotheses on the group, regularity class, and chosen facet notion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extremality concerns convex decomposition, while facetness concerns determination by tight solutions. Facetness implies extremality under the standard theorem; a converse needs extra hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: All compared functions use one fixed group relaxation and normalization.
Facetness is understood through containment of tight feasible-solution sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ facet}\Rightarrow\pi\text{ extreme}\), while the reverse implication requires separate hypotheses.
review_flags: A source is required for the applicable functional facet theorem.
The extreme-to-facet converse varies with the model and regularity assumptions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between convex decomposition and tight-set uniqueness fits the leaf, but the asserted implication from facetness to extremality is a theorem whose applicable model and hypotheses are not sourced. The converse discussion is also explicitly model-dependent, so source verification is necessary.

children.title: Finite–Infinite Group Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Transfer between finite group polyhedra and infinite functional models.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite–Infinite Group Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction of an infinite-group relaxation to a finite subgroup containing the right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\le G\) be a finite subgroup with \(f\in H\). Embedding a finitely supported function on \(H\) into functions on \(G\) by zero extension gives \[R_f(H)=\{y\in R_f(G):\operatorname{supp}(y)\subseteq H\}.\] Consequently, if \(\pi:G\to\mathbb R_+\) is valid for \(R_f(G)\), then its restriction \(\pi|_H\) is valid for the finite-group relaxation \(R_f(H)\). Conversely, a function valid on \(H\) constrains only the supported submodel; extending it validly to all of \(G\) is an additional problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite subgroup model is exactly the portion of the infinite group relaxation supported on that subgroup. Infinite-group validity therefore restricts to finite-group validity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_f(H)=\{y\in R_f(G):\operatorname{supp}(y)\subseteq H\}\) and \(\pi\text{ valid on }G\Rightarrow\pi|_H\text{ valid on }H\).

notation.meaning: finite subgroup of the ambient abelian group

review_flags: No supplied locator treats finite-subgroup restriction of the infinite-group model.
Stronger lifting or extremality-transfer claims require separate hypotheses and sources.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-restriction identity and restriction of validity are correct under the record's group-relaxation definitions and fit the correspondence topic. No source or locator supports this precise finite-subgroup correspondence, however.

children.title: Functional Regularity Classes
children.top_down_role: Continuity, piecewise-linearity, and related analytic classes.

assumptions_latex: Functions on \(G\) are represented by their \(\mathbb Z^k\)-periodic lifts to \(\mathbb R^k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal V_{\mathrm{CPL}}\subseteq\mathcal V_{\mathrm C}\subseteq\mathcal V_{\mathrm B}\subseteq\mathcal V\).

notation.meaning: set of valid functions in the fixed group model

review_flags: No supplied locator covers regularity classes for periodic group-problem functions.
The periodic polyhedral complex is required to be locally finite with finitely many cells modulo integer translations, rather than literally finite on all of \(\mathbb R^k\).
The intended taxonomy may separately distinguish discontinuous piecewise-linear functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard regularity subclasses for periodic valid functions on a real group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(G=\mathbb R^k/\mathbb Z^k\), and identify each function \(\pi:G\to\mathbb R\) with its \(\mathbb Z^k\)-periodic lift to \(\mathbb R^k\). Call \(\pi\) continuous when this lift is continuous. Call \(\pi\) continuous piecewise linear when there is a locally finite \(\mathbb Z^k\)-periodic polyhedral complex covering \(\mathbb R^k\), with finitely many cells modulo integer translations, such that the lift is continuous and affine on every cell. Call \(\pi\) Borel measurable when the inverse image of every open subset of \(\mathbb R\) is Borel. After intersection with the valid-function set \(\mathcal V\), these classes satisfy \[\mathcal V_{\mathrm{CPL}}\subseteq\mathcal V_{\mathrm C}\subseteq\mathcal V_{\mathrm B}\subseteq\mathcal V.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Periodic valid functions may be classified as continuous piecewise linear, continuous, Borel measurable, or unrestricted. For the piecewise-linear class, the periodic complex is locally finite and has finitely many cells up to integer translation. The corresponding classes are nested in that order.

children.title: Extremality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of extremality criteria across functional classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremality in the convex set of normalized valid functions for a fixed group relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal V\) be the convex set of normalized valid functions for a fixed group relaxation, and let \(\pi\in\mathcal V\). The function \(\pi\) is extreme precisely when
\[
\pi=\tfrac12(\pi^1+\pi^2),\quad \pi^1,\pi^2\in\mathcal V
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\pi^1=\pi^2=\pi.
\]
Equivalently, there is no nonzero effective perturbation \(\bar\pi\) for which both \(\pi+\varepsilon\bar\pi\) and \(\pi-\varepsilon\bar\pi\) belong to \(\mathcal V\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\). Thus the extremality boundary is determined by whether the homogeneous equations induced by all tight validity relations admit a nonzero perturbation compatible with the chosen regularity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid function is extreme exactly when it admits no nonzero two-sided perturbation preserving validity and normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ is extreme}\iff\{\bar\pi:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ \pi\pm\varepsilon\bar\pi\in\mathcal V\}=\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: Convex set of normalized valid functions for the fixed relaxation.
Effective perturbation of the valid function.

review_flags: Exact regularity class and group-relaxation model require a supporting extremality reference.
standard_field_rationale: convex-set extremality and effective-perturbation characterization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex-set extremality criterion is standard and the condition kind fits, but the assertion that tight validity relations determine extremality depends on the precise group model, admissible perturbation space, and regularity class. No inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Pathological Function Regimes
children.top_down_role: Irregular generators lying beyond standard classification assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Pathological Function Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity failure caused by unrestricted solutions of additive functional equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If no measurability, local boundedness, or continuity assumption is imposed, the Cauchy equation does not force linearity. Assuming a Hamel basis of \(\mathbb R\) over \(\mathbb Q\), there exists an additive function \(a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[
a(x+y)=a(x)+a(y)
\]
that is not of the form \(a(x)=cx\). Every such non-linear additive function is nonmeasurable, unbounded on every interval, and discontinuous everywhere. Consequently, algebraic additivity relations arising in perturbation tests cannot alone justify continuity, piecewise linearity, or finite-breakpoint descriptions of cut-generating functions or their perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without mild regularity, additive perturbation equations admit everywhere-discontinuous Hamel-basis solutions, invalidating finite-breakpoint or continuity conclusions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R\) is regarded as a vector space over \(\mathbb Q\).
No measurability, local boundedness, or continuity is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(x+y)=a(x)+a(y)\not\Rightarrow \exists c\in\mathbb R\ \forall x\in\mathbb R,\ a(x)=cx.\)

notation.meaning: An additive real function, possibly constructed from a Hamel basis.

review_flags: A functional-equations source and a cut-generating-function perturbation source are needed.
standard_field_rationale: classical pathological solutions of the Cauchy functional equation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classical Cauchy-equation pathology is mathematically standard and fits a failure-boundary leaf, but both the Hamel-basis facts and their application to cut-generating perturbations require specific sources.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lifting of a valid inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-lifting definition for a nonnegative mixed-integer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:=\{x\in\mathbb Z_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^p:Ax\le b\}\), \(N:=\{1,\ldots,n+p\}\), and \(C\subseteq N\). Suppose \(\sum_{j\in C}\alpha_jx_j\le\beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^{n+p}:x_j=0\text{ for all }j\in N\setminus C\}\). The inequality \(\sum_{j=1}^{n+p}\alpha_jx_j\le\beta\) is a lifting of the restricted inequality if it is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifting extends an inequality valid on the coordinate face where variables outside C are zero to an inequality valid on the full mixed-integer hull.
assumptions_latex: \sum_{j\in C}\alpha_jx_j\le\beta\text{ is valid for }\operatorname{conv}(S)\cap\{x:x_j=0\ \forall j\in N\setminus C\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{j=1}^{n+p}\alpha_jx_j\le\beta\text{ is a lifting precisely when it is valid for }\operatorname{conv}(S).

children.title: Minimal Liftings
children.top_down_role: Nondominated extensions of valid functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise minimal extensions from continuous-variable coefficients to integer-variable coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(b\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\mathbb Z^n\) and a valid function \(\psi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) for the continuous group relaxation. A function \(\pi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is a lifting of \(\psi\) if
\[
\sum_r\psi(r)s_r+\sum_p\pi(p)y_p\ge 1
\]
for every finitely supported \(s\in\mathbb R_+^{(\mathbb R^n)}\) and \(y\in\mathbb Z_+^{(\mathbb R^n)}\) satisfying \(\sum_r rs_r+\sum_p py_p\in b+\mathbb Z^n\). The lifting is minimal if every lifting \(\pi'\) with \(\pi'(p)\le\pi(p)\) for all \(p\) satisfies \(\pi'=\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimal lifting is a valid integer-variable extension whose coefficients cannot be decreased pointwise while preserving validity.
assumptions_latex: \(\psi\) is valid for the associated continuous group relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\text{ is minimal}\iff[\pi'\text{ lifting and }\pi'\le\pi\Rightarrow\pi'=\pi].\)

notation.meaning: Valid coefficient function for continuous nonnegative variables.
Coefficient function assigned to nonnegative integer variables.
Affine lattice defining the group relaxation.

review_flags: A standard lifting-theory definition source is required.
standard_field_rationale: pointwise minimal lifting definition for the mixed-integer infinite group relaxation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind are plausible for the mixed-integer infinite-group model, but no lifting-theory citation establishes the exact relaxation, coefficient domains, or pointwise-minimality convention.

children.title: Canonical Lifting Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes in which lifting is canonically determined.

children.title: Unique Liftings
children.top_down_role: Settings where a minimal lifting is uniquely determined.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness among pointwise minimal liftings of a fixed valid function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\psi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be valid for a continuous group relaxation, and let \(\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)\) denote its set of minimal liftings. The function \(\psi\) has the unique-lifting property if
\[
|\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)|=1.
\]
Equivalently, there exists a lifting \(\pi\) such that every minimal lifting \(\pi'\) of \(\psi\) obeys \(\pi'(p)=\pi(p)\) for every \(p\in\mathbb R^n\). Uniqueness here concerns the entire coefficient function, not merely its values on a selected finite set of integer-variable columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid function has a unique lifting when all of its pointwise minimal integer-variable extensions coincide everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(\psi\) admits at least one minimal lifting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)|=1.\)

notation.meaning: Set of all minimal liftings of the valid function.

review_flags: A standard lifting-theory definition source is required.
standard_field_rationale: uniqueness as singleton minimal-lifting set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singleton characterization correctly expresses uniqueness among minimal liftings and the definition kind fits, but the record supplies no inspectable lifting-theory source.

children.title: Trivial Liftings
children.top_down_role: Settings where the canonical lifting requires no nontrivial adjustment.

knowledge_statements.title: Trivial Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical lattice-periodic lifting obtained by minimizing over integer translates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\psi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be a nonnegative valid function for the continuous relaxation associated with \(b+\mathbb Z^n\). Its trivial lifting is the \(\mathbb Z^n\)-periodic function
\[
\pi^*(p):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\psi(p+z),\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n.
\]
Whenever the infimum is attained, \(\pi^*(p)=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\psi(p+z)\). The formula is periodic because \(\pi^*(p+w)=\pi^*(p)\) for every \(w\in\mathbb Z^n\). Its status as a valid or minimal lifting depends on the hypotheses imposed on \(\psi\) and the underlying group model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trivial lifting assigns each point the infimum of the original valid function over all integer translates.
assumptions_latex: \(\psi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R_+\) is valid for the fixed continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi^*(p)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\psi(p+z)\quad\text{and}\quad\pi^*(p+w)=\pi^*(p).\)

notation.meaning: Integer translation vectors in the lattice.

review_flags: Terminology and sufficient hypotheses for validity or minimality vary across lifting models.
A model-specific lifting-theory source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translate-infimum formula is plausible as a representation, but the term “trivial lifting” and the hypotheses under which this function is a valid or minimal lifting vary by model. A model-specific source is necessary.

children.title: Uniqueness–Triviality Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where uniqueness and triviality coincide or separate.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniqueness–Triviality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between uniqueness and a canonical trivial minimal lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\psi\) admit a trivial lifting \(\pi^*\), and suppose \(\pi^*\) is itself minimal. Then \(\psi\) has the unique-lifting property if and only if every minimal lifting equals \(\pi^*\):
\[
|\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)|=1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)=\{\pi^*\}.
\]
Accordingly, in a regime where the trivial lifting is known to be minimal, proving uniqueness reduces to proving that no minimal lifting can differ from \(\pi^*\) at any point. If another minimal lifting differs at one point, uniqueness fails even when both liftings agree on a prescribed finite collection of columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the trivial lifting is minimal, uniqueness holds exactly when it is the only minimal lifting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)|=1\iff\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)=\{\pi^*\}.\)

notation.meaning: Set of minimal liftings of the base valid function.

review_flags: The equivalence is set-theoretic once minimality of the trivial lifting is assumed.
standard_field_rationale: singleton characterization relative to a distinguished member.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Given that the distinguished trivial lifting is minimal, the displayed equivalence is set-theoretically correct and the property kind fits. Nevertheless, no source verifies that this terminology and setup match the intended lifting model.

children.title: Nonunique Liftings
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity and ambiguity among valid extensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicity criterion for minimal extensions of a valid function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A valid function \(\psi\) has nonunique liftings when its minimal-lifting set contains two distinct functions:
\[
\exists\pi^1,\pi^2\in\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi),\quad
\exists p\in\mathbb R^n,
\quad \pi^1(p)\ne\pi^2(p).
\]
Because equality of functions is pointwise, disagreement at a single point is sufficient. If a canonical lifting \(\pi^*\) is minimal, nonuniqueness is equivalently witnessed by a second minimal lifting \(\pi\) and a point \(p\) satisfying \(\pi(p)\ne\pi^*(p)\). This condition distinguishes genuine multiplicity from the existence of several nonminimal valid extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Liftings are nonunique exactly when two pointwise minimal valid extensions differ at at least one point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)|>1\iff\exists\pi^1,\pi^2\in\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi),\ \exists p,\ \pi^1(p)\ne\pi^2(p).\)

notation.meaning: Set of minimal liftings of the base valid function.

review_flags: A standard lifting-theory source is required.
standard_field_rationale: multiplicity criterion for a set of functions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The multiplicity criterion is internally correct and the condition kind matches the leaf, but its lifting-theory terminology and function domain have no inspectable citation.

children.title: Lifting-Region Covering Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric organization of uniqueness and periodicity.

children.title: Lifting Regions
children.top_down_role: Geometric regions controlling admissible lifting values.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifting Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Region on which every minimal lifting is forced to equal the canonical lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\psi\) have a canonical minimal lifting \(\pi^*\), and let \(\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)\) be the set of all minimal liftings. The lifting region associated with \((\psi,\pi^*)\) is
\[
R(\psi):=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:\pi(p)=\pi^*(p)\text{ for every }\pi\in\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)\}.
\]
Thus \(R(\psi)\) is the common-agreement domain on which minimality and validity determine the lifted coefficient uniquely. In geometric models generated by a maximal lattice-free set, this abstract agreement region is represented by a union of spindle-like polyhedra attached to boundary lattice points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lifting region consists of points where every minimal lifting agrees with the chosen canonical minimal lifting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\psi)=\bigcap_{\pi\in\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)}\{p:\pi(p)=\pi^*(p)\}.\)
review_flags: Literature may define the geometric spindle union first and prove the agreement characterization afterward.
A model-specific source is needed to align the abstract and geometric definitions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed common-agreement set is coherent, but lifting regions are often defined geometrically through spindle unions and only later related to forced coefficient values. A model-specific source is needed to determine whether this is the intended definition or a derived property.

children.title: Covering Properties
children.top_down_role: Translational covering behavior of lifting regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Covering Properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lattice-translate covering condition for a lifting region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A lifting region \(R(\psi)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has the covering property with respect to \(\mathbb Z^n\) when
\[
R(\psi)+\mathbb Z^n
:=\{r+z:r\in R(\psi),\ z\in\mathbb Z^n\}
=\mathbb R^n.
\]
Equivalently, every coset of \(\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n\) has a representative in \(R(\psi)\): for every \(p\in\mathbb R^n\), there exists \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) such that \(p-z\in R(\psi)\). This is a global covering condition; overlap among distinct translates is permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifting region covers when its integer translates collectively fill the entire ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\psi)+\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb R^n.\)

notation.meaning: Union of all integer translates of the lifting region.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lattice-translate covering condition and its coset formulation are precise, equivalent, and appropriately classified as a condition, but no lifting-region source is supplied.

children.title: Covering-Based Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Connections between covering behavior and uniqueness of minimal liftings.

knowledge_statements.title: Covering-Based Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique-lifting theorem derived from lattice coverage of the agreement region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\psi\) be a valid function for an affine-lattice group relaxation, let \(\pi^*\) be a canonical minimal lifting, and assume every minimal lifting is \(\mathbb Z^n\)-periodic. If its lifting region satisfies
\[
R(\psi)+\mathbb Z^n=\mathbb R^n,
\]
then \(\psi\) has a unique minimal lifting, namely \(\pi^*\). Indeed, for any \(p\in\mathbb R^n\), coverage supplies \(r\in R(\psi)\) and \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) with \(p=r+z\); periodicity transfers the forced equality at \(r\) to equality at \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If integer translates of the agreement region cover space, periodicity forces every minimal lifting to equal the canonical lifting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L_{\min}(\psi)=\{\pi^*\}.\)

notation.meaning: Region where every minimal lifting equals the canonical lifting.

review_flags: Periodicity and the precise lifting-region agreement theorem require model-specific citation.
The converse, often available for geometric lifting regions, is not asserted here.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The implication follows from the stated agreement-region and periodicity assumptions, and theorem is the correct kind. However, those assumptions require model-specific support, no source is cited, and the sentence beginning “Indeed” is proof text prohibited in a knowledge statement.

children.title: Sequence-Independent Lifting
children.top_down_role: Lifting regimes insensitive to variable-introduction order.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence-Independent Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order invariance of sequentially computed lifted coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{p_1,\ldots,p_k\}\subset\mathbb R^n\) be integer-variable columns, and let a sequential lifting rule assign coefficients by introducing one column at a time. The rule is sequence-independent on \(P\) if, for every permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\), the resulting coefficient vector satisfies
\[
(\pi^{\sigma}(p_1),\ldots,\pi^{\sigma}(p_k))
=(\pi(p_1),\ldots,\pi(p_k))
\]
for a vector independent of \(\sigma\). If the rule always produces minimal liftings and the base function has a unique minimal lifting, then sequence independence holds for every finite \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential lifting is sequence-independent when every ordering of the same columns produces identical final coefficients.
assumptions_latex: The sequential rule is defined for every ordering of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\sigma,\tau,\ \forall p\in P,\ \pi^{\sigma}(p)=\pi^{\tau}(p).\)

notation.meaning: Finite set of columns to be lifted.

review_flags: A specific sequential lifting operator is needed for a stronger algorithmic theorem.
standard_field_rationale: order-independence definition and uniqueness implication.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-invariance definition fits the leaf, but the sequential lifting rule is not specified and it is unclear whether each run produces a complete minimal lifting or only coefficients on the finite set. The uniqueness implication therefore needs a precise operator and supporting source.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Driven Classification Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential facet ceiling for full-dimensional maximal lattice-free convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a full-dimensional maximal lattice-free convex set, meaning \(\operatorname{int}(L)\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\) and no strictly larger convex set has this property. Then \(L\) is a polyhedron and has at most
\[
2^n
\]
facets. Moreover, the relative interior of every facet contains an integer point. The bound shows that the maximum facet count permitted by maximal lattice-freeness grows exponentially with the integer dimension \(n\), even though each fixed-dimensional member has a finite polyhedral description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every full-dimensional maximal lattice-free convex set is polyhedral with at most exponentially many, specifically at most 2^n, facets.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is inclusion-wise maximal with this property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\text{ is a polyhedron and }|\operatorname{facets}(L)|\le 2^n.\)
review_flags: Requires an authoritative locator for the maximal lattice-free polyhedron theorem and its facet bound.
standard_field_rationale: classical parity argument gives the 2^n facet bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polyhedrality, facet-interior lattice-point property, and bound of at most 2^n facets are classical and the complexity-bound kind fits this leaf. An authoritative theorem or page locator is still required; none is supplied.

children.title: Restricted-Family Approximation Limits
children.top_down_role: Strength limitations of prescribed lattice-free families.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Family Approximation Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal boundary for closures generated by a prescribed subfamily of lattice-free cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(S\subseteq R\) be the intended integer-feasible set, and let \(\mathcal L_0\subseteq\mathcal L\) be families of valid lattice-free inequalities for \(S\). Define \(C(\mathcal F)=R\cap\bigcap_{(a,\beta)\in\mathcal F}\{x:a^Tx\le\beta\}\). Then \(C(\mathcal L)\subseteq C(\mathcal L_0)\). Moreover, if some \((a,\beta)\in\mathcal L\) cuts a point \(\bar x\in C(\mathcal L_0)\), then \(C(\mathcal L)\subsetneq C(\mathcal L_0)\); hence the restricted family cannot reproduce the full lattice-free closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted lattice-free family gives a weaker closure, strictly weaker whenever an omitted cut removes a point surviving every retained cut.
assumptions_latex: Every inequality indexed by \(\mathcal L\) is valid for \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C(\mathcal L)\subseteq C(\mathcal L_0)\), with strict inclusion under the displayed witness condition.

notation.meaning: closure obtained by imposing all inequalities in family F on R

review_flags: Exact intended restricted lattice-free family is unspecified by the node path.
A family-specific approximation theorem or lower bound is still required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusion is a correct set-theoretic consequence of family containment, but it does not establish the family-specific approximation limitation required by this leaf. The prescribed lattice-free family and a supporting approximation theorem or lower bound are missing.

children.title: Lattice-Free Cut Access Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational barriers to accessing effective lattice-free cuts.

children.title: Lattice-Free Cut Separation
children.top_down_role: Complexity of finding violated cuts from lattice-free families.

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice-Free Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle formulation of separation over a specified lattice-free cut family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rational relaxation \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a point \(\bar x\in R\), and an implicitly represented family \(\mathcal L\) of lattice-free inequalities \(a^Tx\le\beta\) valid for the intended integer-feasible set. A separation algorithm either returns an encoded pair \((a,\beta)\in\mathcal L\) satisfying \(a^T\bar x>\beta\), or returns the certificate \(a^T\bar x\le\beta\) for every \((a,\beta)\in\mathcal L\). Thus its negative answer certifies membership of \(\bar x\) in the \(\mathcal L\)-closure of \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separation finds any lattice-free-family inequality violated by the query point or certifies that no such violated inequality exists.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal L\) is valid for the intended integer-feasible set.
Membership and output encodings for \(\mathcal L\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a violated member of \(\mathcal L\) or a certificate that \(\bar x\in C(\mathcal L)\).
review_flags: The oracle specification is standard, but no supplied locator directly treats separation over lattice-free families.
Complexity depends on the representation of the admissible lattice-free sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This specifies a separation oracle rather than an implementable algorithm for an arbitrary implicitly represented family. Existence, computability, and complexity depend on the representation of the lattice-free family, for which no supporting source or sufficient assumptions are supplied.

children.title: Lattice-Free Cut Selection
children.top_down_role: Complexity of choosing effective forbidden regions or cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Lattice-Free Cut Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection of a strongest scored cut from an explicitly available candidate family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a point \(\bar x\), a finite nonempty candidate set \(F\) of lattice-free inequalities \(a_i^Tx\le\beta_i\), and a positive normalization \(s(a_i)>0\). Compute \(v_i=(a_i^T\bar x-\beta_i)/s(a_i)\). If \(\max_{i\in F}v_i\le0\), output “no violated candidate”; otherwise output any \(i^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{i\in F}v_i\) and its inequality. The selected cut maximizes normalized violation over \(F\), with ties resolved by a fixed deterministic rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given finitely many candidates, select a violated lattice-free cut having maximum normalized violation, or report that none is violated.
assumptions_latex: Each candidate inequality is valid for the intended integer-feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a violated candidate exists, the output attains \(\max_{i\in F}(a_i^T\bar x-\beta_i)/s(a_i)\).

notation.meaning: positive scaling used to normalize violation

children.title: Selection–Separation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where identifying a useful cut differs from ordinary separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection–Separation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete infinite-family gap between finding a violation and attaining the best violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=\mathbb R\), query \(\bar x=1\), and consider the valid inequalities \(x\le 1/k\) indexed by integers \(k\ge2\), with score equal to raw violation. Separation is immediate: for example, \(x\le1/2\) is violated. Yet the candidate violations are \(1-1/k\); their supremum is \(1\), but no index attains it. Consequently a separation oracle can return a violated cut although the corresponding exact best-cut selection problem has no solution unless compactness, finiteness, or an attainment condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infinite family may admit easy separation while having no maximally violated member, so exact best-cut selection is not automatically available.
assumptions_latex: The candidate family may be infinite.
Cut quality is measured by raw violation at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A violated inequality exists, but \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{k\ge2}(1-1/k)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: integer index of a candidate inequality

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding length of rational vertices in an integer-hull generator description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational vertex \(v\in\mathbb Q^n\), choose the unique representation \(v=p/q\) with \(p\in\mathbb Z^n\), \(q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(p_1,\ldots,p_n,q)=1\). Its binary encoding length is \(\ell_V(v)=\ell(q)+\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(p_j)\), where \(\ell(t)=1+\lceil\log_2(|t|+1)\rceil\) includes a sign bit. For a finite vertex set \(V\), set \(\ell_V(V)=\sum_{v\in V}\ell_V(v)\), plus the conventional list delimiters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational vertex is encoded by primitive integer numerators and a positive common denominator; total vertex encoding is the summed binary length.
assumptions_latex: A common-denominator binary encoding is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_V(v)=\ell(q)+\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(p_j)\) for the primitive representation \(v=p/q\).

notation.meaning: primitive common-denominator representation of a rational vertex
signed binary length of an integer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial encoding bound for mixed-integer-hull vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity bound for vertices of the convex hull of a nonnegative rational mixed-integer linear set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}, G\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times p}, b\in\mathbb{Q}^m, and S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p:Ax+Gy\le b,\ x\ge0,\ y\ge0\}. If every coefficient of (A,G,b) has encoding size at most L, then every vertex of \operatorname{conv}(S) has encoding size bounded by a polynomial in n+p and L.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative rational mixed-integer linear set whose coefficient encodings have size at most L, every vertex of its convex hull has encoding size polynomial in n+p and L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall v\in\operatorname{vert}(\operatorname{conv}(S)),\quad \operatorname{enc}(v)\le\operatorname{poly}(n+p,L).

knowledge_statements.title: Ray Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-invariant binary encoding of rational extreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational ray \(\rho=\{\lambda r:\lambda\ge 0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has a unique primitive integral generator \(r\in\rho\cap(\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\})\) satisfying \(\gcd(|r_1|,\ldots,|r_n|)=1\). Define \(\ell_R(\rho)=\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(r_j)\), where \(\ell(t)=1+\lceil\log_2(|t|+1)\rceil\). For a finite ray set \(D\), define \(\ell_R(D)=\sum_{\rho\in D}\ell_R(\rho)\), apart from fixed list-format overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational ray is represented by the unique primitive integer generator pointing along that ray, and its size is the total binary length of the generator coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a rational one-dimensional cone.
The generator is required to lie in \(\rho\), which fixes its direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_R(\rho)=\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(r_j)\) for the unique primitive integral generator \(r\in\rho\).

notation.meaning: primitive integral generator lying in the ray

knowledge_statements.title: Generator-Encoding Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined size accounting for vertex–ray descriptions of rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a rational polyhedron have a generator representation \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(D)\), where \(V\subseteq\mathbb Q^n\) is finite and \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) is a finite set of primitive integral ray generators. Define \(\ell_V(V)=\sum_{v\in V}\ell_V(v)\), \(\ell_R(D)=\sum_{r\in D}\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(r_j)\), and \(L_G(P;V,D)=\ell_V(V)+\ell_R(D)\), apart from fixed list-format overhead. Consequently, generator count alone does not determine description length: both the number of generators and their coordinate bit lengths contribute to \(L_G(P;V,D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The encoding length of a vertex–ray representation is the sum of the encoded vertex and ray-generator lengths, so generator count alone does not determine its size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_G(P;V,D)=\ell_V(V)+\ell_R(D)\), so total encoding length depends on both generator count and coordinate bit lengths.

notation.meaning: finite set of rational point generators
finite set of primitive integral ray generators

knowledge_statements.title: Facet Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary description length of primitive rational facet inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a full-dimensional rational polyhedron and let \(a^Tx\le b\) define a facet. Clearing denominators and dividing all coefficients by their greatest common divisor gives the unique primitive pair \((a,b)\in\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb Z\) with the orientation valid for \(P\). For \(t\in\mathbb Z\), define \(\ell(t)=1+\lceil\log_2(|t|+1)\rceil\), and define the facet encoding length by \(\ell_F(a,b)=\ell(b)+\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(a_j)\). The length of an irredundant facet description is the sum of these lengths, apart from fixed matrix and list-format overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each rational facet is encoded by its uniquely oriented primitive integer coefficients, and its size is their total signed binary length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell_F(a,b)=\ell(b)+\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(a_j)\) for the primitive facet pair oriented to be valid for \(P\).

notation.meaning: primitive integral facet coefficients oriented to be valid for P
signed binary length of an integer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial encoding bound for mixed-integer-hull facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient bit-length of facet-defining inequalities for a rational mixed-integer system with nonnegative variables.

children.title: Smallest Perfect Formulations
children.top_down_role: Size minimization for exact original-space descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Smallest Perfect Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-size exact linear description in the original variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), an original-space perfect formulation is a finite rational system \(Ax\le b\), together with equations defining \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\), whose solution set is exactly \(P\). Its inequality size is the number of nonredundant rows of \(A\). The smallest perfect-formulation size \(\operatorname{pf}(P)\) is the minimum of this number over all such systems using only \(x\). If \(P\) is full-dimensional, \(\operatorname{pf}(P)\) equals the number of facets of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest perfect formulation is an exact original-space linear description with the fewest nonredundant inequalities; for full-dimensional polyhedra it has one inequality per facet.
assumptions_latex: Affine-hull equations are counted separately from inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P\) is full-dimensional, then \(\operatorname{pf}(P)=f_{n-1}(P)\).

notation.meaning: minimum number of inequalities in an exact original-space formulation
number of facets of an n-dimensional polyhedron P

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Multiplier Characterization of Valid Polytope Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Farkas-type validity characterization for a positive-dimensional polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) be a polytope with \(\dim(P)\ge1\). An inequality \(cx\le\delta\) is valid for \(P\) if and only if there exists a nonnegative row vector \(u\) such that \[uA=c\qquad\text{and}\qquad ub=\delta.\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary-Indexed Correlation-Polytope Inequality and Vertex Slack
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States both validity over the entire correlation polytope and the exact slack at each binary rank-one vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\), \[\left\langle 2\operatorname{Diag}(a)-aa^T,Y\right\rangle\le 1\qquad\text{for every }Y\in P_n^{\mathrm{corr}}.\] Moreover, for every \(b\in\{0,1\}^n\), the slack at the vertex \(Y=bb^T\) is \[1-\left\langle 2\operatorname{Diag}(a)-aa^T,bb^T\right\rangle=(1-a^Tb)^2.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every binary vector a defines a valid inequality for the correlation polytope. At a vertex bbᵀ, its slack is exactly (1−aᵀb)².

children.title: Extension Complexity
children.top_down_role: Size of formulations using auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Extension Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum number of inequalities in any linear extended formulation of a polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polytope. An extension of \(P\) is a polyhedron \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+k}:A x+B y\le d\}\) whose projection onto the \(x\)-coordinates equals \(P\). The extension complexity \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\) is the minimum number of inequalities in such a system, over every \(k\ge0\) and every rational extended formulation; equations may be eliminated or counted separately. Thus \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\le\operatorname{pf}(P)\) by taking \(k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension complexity is the fewest inequalities needed to describe a higher-dimensional polyhedron that projects exactly onto the target polytope.
assumptions_latex: Only exact linear extended formulations are admitted.
Affine equations are counted separately or eliminated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{m:P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q),\ Q\text{ has }m\text{ inequalities}\}\le\operatorname{pf}(P)\).

source_refs.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

review_flags: Equation-counting convention should be standardized across extension-complexity records.

source_witnesses.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

children.title: Projection Complexity
children.top_down_role: Cost and structural effects of eliminating auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary-dimension cost under a prescribed inequality budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and an integer budget \(m\ge\operatorname{xc}(P)\), define its projection complexity at budget \(m\) by \(\operatorname{pc}_m(P)=\min\{k\ge0:\exists Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+k}\text{ described by at most }m\text{ inequalities with }P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\}\). This measures the least auxiliary dimension needed when the extension may use at most \(m\) inequalities. It is nonincreasing in \(m\), and \(\operatorname{pc}_m(P)=0\) whenever \(m\ge\operatorname{pf}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed inequality budget, projection complexity is the minimum number of auxiliary variables needed for an exact projecting formulation.
assumptions_latex: Only exact linear projections are admitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(m_1\le m_2\), then \(\operatorname{pc}_{m_2}(P)\le\operatorname{pc}_{m_1}(P)\), and \(m\ge\operatorname{pf}(P)\) implies \(\operatorname{pc}_m(P)=0\).

notation.meaning: minimum auxiliary dimension at budget m

source_refs.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105
2.2.3 When Is the Projection of a Facet a Facet of the Projection? p. 29

children.title: Extension–Projection Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among auxiliary dimension, inequality count, and projected description size.

knowledge_statements.title: Extension–Projection Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto frontier between inequality count and auxiliary dimension in exact extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\mathcal E(P)\) contain every pair \((m,k)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^2\) for which an exact extension in \(n+k\) variables has at most \(m\) inequalities. The extension–projection frontier is the set of componentwise minimal pairs in \(\mathcal E(P)\). The set \(\mathcal E(P)\) is upward closed: if \((m,k)\in\mathcal E(P)\), then \((m',k')\in\mathcal E(P)\) for all \(m'\ge m\) and \(k'\ge k\), because unused variables may be added and the same formulation has at most any larger inequality budget. Hence its minimal pairs encode all nondominated inequality-count and auxiliary-dimension tradeoffs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The frontier consists of achievable exact formulations whose inequality count and auxiliary dimension cannot be simultaneously improved componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The componentwise minimal elements of \(\mathcal E(P)\) form its nondominated extension–projection frontier.

notation.meaning: set of achievable inequality-budget and auxiliary-dimension pairs

children.title: Integer Feasibility Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A direct witness for rational linear integer feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\). For the system \(Ax\le b\), \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), an integer-feasibility certificate is a vector \(z\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) satisfying \(Az\le b\). Verification consists of checking integrality of every coordinate of \(z\) and all rational inequalities. If the binary encoding length of \(z\) is polynomial in the input length of \((A,b)\), then the certificate is a polynomially verifiable witness in the standard bit model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-size integer vector satisfying every inequality is a directly checkable certificate that the integer system is feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b\) are rational and binary encoded.
The proposed vector \(z\) has finite binary encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}\), so the integer system is feasible.

notation.meaning: binary encoding of the data and witness

children.title: Integer Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Algebraic, geometric, and cutting-plane witnesses of integer infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite Chvátal–Gomory derivation certifying absence of integer points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational system \(Ax\le b\), a cutting-plane infeasibility certificate is a finite sequence of valid inequalities. Each line is either an original row or is obtained from earlier lines by taking a nonnegative rational combination whose resulting left-hand side is integral and then rounding down the right-hand side. If the final line is \(0\le-1\), every integer vector satisfying the original system would satisfy a contradiction. The sequence is verifiable by checking every multiplier, integrality condition, rounding step, and the terminal inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A checkable sequence of valid integer rounding cuts ending in a contradiction certifies that the rational system has no integer solution.
assumptions_latex: Every derivation multiplier is nonnegative and rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb{Z}^n:Ax\le b\}=\varnothing\).
review_flags: A precise authoritative locator for Chvatal–Gomory refutation certificates is required.
Completeness and certificate-size bounds are intentionally not asserted.

children.title: Integrality Certificates
children.top_down_role: TU, TDI, Hilbert-basis, and decomposition-based witnesses.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total unimodularity as a sufficient, polynomially checkable integrality witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) be totally unimodular and let \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\). Then every vertex of \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is integral; equivalently, \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\) when \(P\) contains no lines, with the corresponding recession directions treated integrally in the general case. Thus a verifiable recognition certificate that \(A\) is totally unimodular, together with the integrality of \(b\), certifies the integrality of the polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total unimodularity of the constraint matrix and integrality of the right-hand side certify that all vertices of the polyhedron are integral.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is an integer totally unimodular matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex of \(P\) lies in \(\mathbb{Z}^n\).

notation.meaning: polyhedron defined by the certified system

review_flags: Authoritative theorem and total-unimodularity recognition locators are missing.
The vertex-integrality conclusion is standard; the unbounded integer-hull formulation needs source review.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The total-unimodularity vertex conclusion is standard, but no source is supplied, and the claimed integer-hull equivalence with lineality and recession directions requires authoritative verification.

children.title: Nonintegrality Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Fractional vertices, holes, and matrix or system obstructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonintegrality Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fractional vertex as a locally checkable obstruction to polyhedral integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) with rational data. A fractional-vertex obstruction consists of \(v\in\,P\setminus\mathbb{Z}^n\) and an index set \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that \(A_Iv=b_I\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A_I)=n\). Feasibility verifies \(v\in P\), a fractional coordinate verifies \(v\notin\mathbb{Z}^n\), and the rank condition verifies that \(v\) is a vertex. Hence \(P\) is not an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible fractional point fixed uniquely by full-rank active constraints is a checkable fractional vertex and proves the polyhedron is nonintegral.
assumptions_latex: The displayed point and active-row set are rationally encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is a nonintegral vertex of \(P\), and therefore \(P\ne\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\).

notation.meaning: indices of a full-rank collection of constraints active at v
rows and right-hand sides indexed by I

review_flags: A source locator for the fractional-vertex characterization of nonintegrality is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A feasible fractional point with full-rank active rows is a suitable obstruction, but the record supplies no source for the vertex characterization and resulting nonintegrality claim.

children.title: Integer-Hull Optimization
children.top_down_role: Exact linear optimization over the integer hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear optimization access to a rational integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define its integer hull by \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\). An exact optimization oracle receives \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and returns a point \(x^*\in P_I\) satisfying \(c^\mathsf{T}x^*=\max\{c^\mathsf{T}x:x\in P_I\}\), or reports that \(P_I\) is empty or that the objective is unbounded above. The oracle output includes the applicable status and, when the optimum is finite, an optimizing point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer-hull optimization oracle maximizes a rational linear objective over the convex hull of integer feasible points and reports emptiness or unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output correctly identifies emptiness, unboundedness, or an optimizer \(x^*\) over \(P_I\).

children.title: Integer-Hull Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation of points from the integer hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact strong separation access to a rational integer hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and the integer hull \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\), a strong separation oracle either confirms \(y\,\in P_I\) or returns \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\) such that \(a^\mathsf{T}x\le\beta\) for every \(x\in P_I\) while \(a^\mathsf{T}y>\beta\). Thus the returned inequality is valid for every integer feasible point and strictly excludes the query point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle either confirms integer-hull membership or returns a rational valid inequality strictly violated by the query point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(y\in P_I\), or the returned inequality strongly separates \(y\) from \(P_I\).

notation.meaning: integer hull of the underlying polyhedron

children.title: Integer-Hull Oracle Equivalence

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Hull Oracle Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial oracle equivalence for rational, well-described integer hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_I\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty rational polyhedron with known polynomial bounds on facet encoding length. In the rational bit model, exact linear optimization over \(P_I\) and exact strong separation for \(P_I\) are polynomial-time oracle reducible to one another. Consequently, a polynomial-time implementation of either oracle yields a polynomial-time implementation of the other, with running time polynomial in the dimension, query encoding length, and the stated facet-complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a well-described rational integer hull, exact optimization and strong separation can simulate one another in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: A polynomial facet-encoding bound for \(P_I\) is available.
Computation uses exact rational arithmetic in the bit model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{OPT}(P_I)\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathrm{SEP}(P_I)\).

children.title: Closure Membership Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Membership Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership access for a specified polyhedral closure operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a closure operator \(\mathcal{C}\) that maps a rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) to a closed convex set \(\mathcal{C}(P)\). The exact closure-membership problem receives an encoding of \(P\) and a rational point \(y\), and returns YES exactly when \(y\in\mathcal{C}(P)\). Its bit complexity is measured in the encoding lengths of \(P\), \(y\), and any parameters defining \(\mathcal{C}\); no uniform polynomial bound follows without specifying the closure family and representation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure membership decides whether a rational query point belongs to a specified closure; its complexity depends on the closure and input representation.
assumptions_latex: The closure operator \(\mathcal{C}\) and its parameters are fixed or included in the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is YES if and only if \(y\in\mathcal{C}(P)\).

notation.meaning: closed convex relaxation produced by the chosen closure operator

A source treating closure-access complexity is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Separation Complexity

Complexity is measured in the bit lengths of \(P\), \(y\), closure parameters, and the separating inequality. A polynomial bound requires structural and encoding assumptions on the particular closure.

assumptions_latex: The input data and requested separator are rationally encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output certifies membership or strongly separates \(y\) from \(\mathcal{C}(P)\).

children.title: Closure Access Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions, equivalence regimes, and gaps between the two access modes.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Access Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic exact and weak-oracle reductions for closed convex closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathcal{C}(P)\) be closed and convex. One call to an exact strong-separation oracle decides exact membership in \(K\). Conversely, exact membership alone does not generally supply a separating hyperplane. If \(K\) is full-dimensional, contained between known concentric rational balls of radii \(r\) and \(R\), and access is formulated with rational tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), then weak membership and weak separation are polynomial-time oracle reducible to one another, with complexity polynomial in the input length and \(\log(R/(r\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong separation immediately decides membership; the reverse requires weak-oracle tolerances and geometric radius bounds for polynomial equivalence.
assumptions_latex: For the reverse weak reduction, known rational radii satisfy \(B(z,r)\subseteq K\subseteq B(z,R)\).
The tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is positive and rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{SEP}_{\mathrm{exact}}(K)\) yields \(\mathrm{MEM}_{\mathrm{exact}}(K)\) in one query, and \(\mathrm{WMEM}(K)\equiv_{\mathrm{poly}}\mathrm{WSEP}(K)\) under the stated bounds.

notation.meaning: Euclidean ball centered at z with radius r
weak membership and weak separation problems

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Polyhedral Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite rational inequality representation and its encoding size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit description of a rational polyhedron \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a finite system \(Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\). Its description length is the total binary encoding length of all coefficients, together with dimensions and row delimiters. This representation permits direct membership testing by evaluating all \(m\) inequalities, in time polynomial in the description length and the query-point encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit polyhedral description lists finitely many rational inequalities; its size is their binary encoding length and it directly supports membership tests.
assumptions_latex: All coefficients and query coordinates are rational and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(Q\) is decidable by checking \(Ax\le b\) in polynomial bit time.

children.title: Oracle Descriptions

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit exact rational access through membership, strong-separation, or linear-optimization queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact oracle description of a convex set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) represents \(Q\) through a query procedure rather than an explicit list of inequalities or vertices. A membership oracle receives \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and decides whether \(y\in Q\). A strong-separation oracle receives \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and either confirms \(y\in Q\) or returns \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\) such that \(a^\mathsf{T}x\le\beta<a^\mathsf{T}y\) for every \(x\in Q\). A linear-optimization oracle receives \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and returns an optimizer of \(c^\mathsf{T}x\) over \(Q\), or the applicable empty or unbounded status. Complexity counts ordinary computation and the number, encoding lengths, and costs of oracle calls. Approximate oracle descriptions require separately specified tolerances and guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact oracle description provides rational membership, strong-separation, or linear-optimization queries instead of listing a complete representation; approximate variants require explicit tolerance rules.
assumptions_latex: Queries and returned certificates use specified rational encodings.
The stated interfaces are exact; approximate variants are treated under a separately declared oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The set \(Q\) is accessed through the declared oracle interface without requiring an explicit facet or vertex list.

children.title: Description–Oracle Conversion Gaps

knowledge_statements.title: Description–Oracle Conversion Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential gap between separation access and an original-space facet description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 4\), let \(P_n=\operatorname{conv}\{(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)):\pi\in S_n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). A strong separation oracle for \(P_n\) runs in polynomial time by sorting the coordinates of the query point and checking the majorization inequalities. However, every irredundant original-space description contains the equality \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=n(n+1)/2\) and one facet inequality \(\sum_{i\in S}x_i\ge |S|(|S|+1)/2\) for every nonempty proper subset \(S\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Thus polynomial-time oracle access need not yield a polynomial-size explicit description in the same variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permutahedra have efficient separation oracles but exponentially many original-space facets, so oracle access cannot generally be converted into a compact explicit description.
assumptions_latex: Descriptions use only the original \(n\) coordinates, without auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_n\) has polynomial-time strong separation but \(2^n-2\) subset-facet inequalities.

notation.meaning: The permutahedron generated by permutations of 1 through n.
The symmetric group on n elements.

children.title: Restricted-Family Oracle Barriers
